## Water privatisation is not destiny: Uruguay's referendum on the right to water

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-24-witness-供水私有化不是宿命-乌拉圭公投的水权胜利/
- show: Witness History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/witness/)
- original episode: Uruguay's water referendum
- published: 2026-08-24 · duration: 10:12
- transcript: Machine transcription · 1606 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**On 31 October 2004, Uruguayans voted 64.7% in favour of writing ‘water is a natural resource essential to life’ into the constitution, and of restricting water supply to the state alone — making Uruguay the first country in the world to lock water privatisation out at constitutional level. The movement began with a tap being shut off in a coastal city.**

why listen: The information density is moderate, but the story of how a grassroots movement levered signatures, horseback riders and a cup of mate into a constitutional amendment is worth studying for anyone organising around a public-interest issue.

### points

[0:45] (Carmen Soa) **The right to water was won in the streets, not at a negotiating table** — The referendum result came in on 31 October 2004: 64.7% of Uruguayan voters backed amending the constitution to write the right to water into the country's foundational law. Carmen Soa, who was there, remembers the street outside the union hall blocked solid with people after polls closed — dancing, phoning their families, discarded ballot papers drifting through the air. This was not a victory produced by elite negotiation but a street-level popular movement, and even the people inside the union offices were swept up in it.

[1:30] **The amendment did not just grant a right, it bolted the door on privatisation** — The referendum amended the constitution to add the phrase ‘water is a natural resource essential to life’, and went further: drinking water and sanitation could be provided by the state exclusively, not by private companies. That made Uruguay the first country in the world to write the principle of public water provision into its constitution. The amendment did more than put a human right into the text — it directly foreclosed the possibility of any future government handing water supply to private firms by statute.

[2:40] **Privatisation raised prices and shut off the free taps too** — The movement's origins go back to the 1990s. The coastal region of Maldonado granted a water concession to a private company for the first time — the first such concession since 1952. The government argued private investment was needed to upgrade the pipe network and meet growing demand; the company said it needed rate increases to finance the infrastructure. But activists pointed out that connection charges rose sharply and households that could not pay were cut off, while free taps in public spaces such as town squares and schools were shut down as well, hitting the poorest families living in informal housing hardest.

[4:00] (Carmen Soa) **With no money for advertising, 10% in signatures can still force a referendum** — In 2002, civic groups and unions formed the Commission in Defence of Water and Life and launched a national signature drive. Under Uruguay's electoral rules, collecting signatures from 10% of registered voters obliges the electoral authority to hold a referendum. Carmen says they handed out leaflets in markets under the slogans ‘water belongs to everyone’ and ‘water is life’; with no money for media advertising, all they could do was go door to door. Within a year they had 283,000 signatures, far above the threshold.

[5:10] **Remote villages were only reached because 23 people rode there on horseback** — To carry the campaign to the most remote parts of the country, 23 union comrades set out on horseback in early October, crossing Uruguay and reaching small villages where there had been almost no organised presence before. On 31 October they rode up to the Legislative Palace in the capital, Montevideo, which drew wide media coverage. This long ride turned referendum campaigning into a symbolically charged social event, and it stitched rural and urban organising together.

[6:00] (TV commercial narration) **A cup of mate turned a constitutional right into an everyday scene** — Two days before the vote, supporters paid out of their own pockets for a television advert: a man holding a mate, with a voiceover saying ‘privatise water and you won't have water for your mate. Access to water is a basic human right — vote yes.’ By using Uruguay's national drink as the metaphor, the advert turned an abstract constitutional right into a daily domestic scene. It is a textbook case of grassroots organising using a cultural symbol to move people, and of creativity compensating for a thin budget.

[7:30] (Carmen Soa) **64.7% turned a small country's referendum into an international event** — Carmen went to vote at midday and then headed to the union building, where about seven television sets had been showing election coverage since eight in the morning. That evening the result came through: 64.7% in favour. The union's phones were overwhelmed; she says she was so busy that at times she could not tell which country or which language a call was coming from, because the vote had generated enormous international attention. The celebrations and press coverage turned a constitutional amendment in a small country into a milestone for the global water-rights movement.

[8:08] (Carmen Soa) **Water is not a commodity: at least 30 countries followed it into their constitutions** — Since Uruguay's referendum, at least 30 countries have written the right to water into their constitutions, and in 2010 the UN General Assembly formally recognised access to water and sanitation as a human right. Carmen sums it up: water is a human right because without water there is no life — like air, you must have it whether or not you have money. That line captures the ethical core of the whole movement: water is not a commodity but the precondition for life, and it cannot be handed over to the logic of profit.

## Only 60 of the 5,000 People on a Carrier Fight; the Rest Restock Vending Machines

**On a U.S. carrier after 9/11, only fifty or sixty of the 5,000 people aboard ever touch a bomb. Everyone else spends the war restocking vending machines, doing laundry, and passing rumors — while the captain's biggest worry is whether his sailors are watching the news.**

why listen: This episode reduces war to a job: tedious, young, institutional. For anyone who thinks about organizational management and what motivates young people, it is more honest material than any war film.

### points

[0:00] **War on a carrier is shift work, not a charge into battle** — The episode sets its tone with a 20-year-old sailor who restocks the vending machines: twelve hours a day of nothing but snacks, and in months at sea he has been up on the deck exactly twice. Of the more than 5,000 people aboard the carrier, only fifty or sixty actually drop bombs. The overwhelming majority do laundry, cook, fix machinery, and move supplies. For them the war is not a charge; it is a rotating shift. From this the show draws its central judgment: turning your life upside down to go fight is one thing, and giving up everything to restock vending machines twelve hours a day is another.

[12:42] **What enlisted her was not patriotism but a 15-second commercial** — Jessica Phillips had been working at a Barnes & Noble in Florida, living inside the ‘black hole’ of a small town. One night she ran away from home with no money, and at a party she said offhandedly that she was going home to enlist. What actually triggered it was a 15-second Navy commercial — the carrier, the fighter jets, ‘this is our classroom’. The thought came to her on a Friday; by Wednesday she was in boot camp. Her story shows what a military with an average age of 21 often runs on: not patriotism, but a passing impulse and the urge to escape where you are.

[20:00] **The most sensitive subject aboard is not the war, it is sex** — Rumor is the ship's number one entertainment: when they will make port, who gets to go home early, who slept with whom. The distortions get far enough that someone hears he is in love with a person he has never met. The producer took this seriously and asked one sailor about it in the laundry room; within minutes it had traveled up the chain of command and reached the executive officer. Because the Tailhook scandal was only 10 years earlier and women had been serving on combat ships for only 8 years, relations between the sexes are the highest-sensitivity zone aboard. The XO narrows the definition of dating down to ‘walking side by side with your heads leaning together’, and requires a gap of at least two butt-widths.

[27:16] **He did not volunteer; a judge gave him two options** — Kevin Rann is not here out of patriotism. Facing a 7-year sentence in Texas, he was given a choice by the judge: prison or the military. He picked the Navy, and his job is eight-hour patrol shifts, catching people drinking, fighting, and having sex. He calls the carrier a ‘prison on water’ and says he has no intention of changing. The public affairs officer escorting the interview had a stomachache the whole time. This thread exposes something outside the patriotism narrative: court-compelled enlistment is also a source of manpower.

[31:24] **Only a third of the sailors can name the Secretary of State** — Captain James McDonald knows exactly how young his people are. Every day he reads international news over the ship's public address system, tying each person's job to the war as a whole. Asking sailors on watch at random: who is the Secretary of State? Only a third get it right. Who is the Secretary of Defense? Slightly better, but not by much. His conclusion: young people only look at their own small world, and it is the captain's job to help them see the larger mosaic. Then comes the fresh-water push — showers under two minutes each, delivered in the tone of a high school football coach.

[38:27] **The dangerous part is not dropping the bomb, it is getting back on deck** — Takeoff comes from a catapult; landing means catching one of four steel cables on the flight deck with a tailhook. Captain Ross Myers has watched 6 friends die in landing crashes over 16 years, with no survivors. Every pilot carries a ‘blood chit’ — a plea for help written in Arabic, English and other languages: ‘I am an American, I will not harm you, please provide food, water, shelter and medical care’. Together with 20 to 25 pounds of survival gear, flying a fighter is not showing off; it is a procedure that could kill you on any given run.

[44:56] **Pilots do not need to hate the enemy, only to complete the mission** — Two pilots' views of Afghanistan contradict each other. One says that flying over the target, ‘it's just sand and rocks down there, nothing worth fighting for’; the other finds the world beautiful from the air but has to keep yanking himself back to the mission. Asked whether dropping bombs carries a moral weight, one answer is ‘it's my job, and I feel no guilt about dropping bombs on the people below’; the other calls it ‘a double-edged emotion — you train your whole life and you finally got it right’. The show treats this — that the people carrying it out need not hate the enemy, only finish the task — as the key to understanding the war machine.

[53:26] **The proof of hegemony is 12 sandwiches nobody ordered** — Late at night, a serviceman brings out 12 chicken sandwiches, unasked, for 4 people who are eating cereal. Ira says this is the real essence of American military supremacy: not the carrier itself, but this surplus of attention — giving every pilot the fastest jet and the most accurate bombs, and on top of that an endless supply of chicken sandwiches, chairs with nicknames on them, and a rehearsal room for the band. ‘Other countries don't even get a chance.’ The observation pulls the whole episode back from personal stories to the logic of a national machine.

## Screens train multitasking, not learning: the harder classrooms digitize, the worse kids do

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-iq2-技术不等于学习-屏幕正在让一代人变笨/
- show: Intelligence Squared (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/iq2/)
- original episode: Is Tech Making Our Kids Less Capable? With Dr Jared Cooney Horvath
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 33:14
- transcript: Machine transcription · 7059 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The harder classrooms have pushed digital tools since 2010, the further children's cognition and digital literacy have fallen across the board; screens train multitasking rather than learning, and AI only makes the errors harder to see.**

why listen: The episode supplies checkable numbers and a mechanism, turning "screens damage the brain" from a feeling into a chain of evidence; useful if you have to take a public position or build a product in this space.

### points

[1:56] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **The more technology you push into a classroom, the less kids learn** — Jared defines the ‘digital illusion’ as the default assumption that technology equals learning. From 2010 onward, schools brought in education technology at scale, expecting it to deliver more information, unlock creativity, and free students from rote memorization. The data say the opposite: people are simply not good at learning from technology, and the more technology you inject into a classroom, the more sharply learning development and cognitive ability decline. It can be a tool for producing work, but it is not a tool for the classroom.

[6:09] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **The one skill school actually trains to mastery is multitasking** — The first mechanism of learning is attention, and multitasking lowers both accuracy and speed at the same time while pushing memory into a secondary network. But a computer is a multitasking machine by design: children spend more than 2,500 hours a year multitasking on computers, and doing homework at home they start drifting after an average of 6 minutes. Even in a classroom with a teacher watching, 24 to 38 minutes of every hour go to being off-task. By the ten-thousand-hour rule, four years of this makes them expert at exactly one thing — multitasking.

[8:29] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **Text without page numbers gives memory nothing to hold on to** — Human memory leans heavily on spatial location: a book's fixed three-dimensional coordinates become the cue for retrieval, which is why after finishing one you can roughly recall which page a passage sat on. On a screen, text flows in at the bottom and out at the top; three-dimensional position is erased, and that entire dimension of memory is discarded. After about four or five minutes the brain starts signaling ‘I'm not receiving this’, and the reader stops reading deeply and switches to scanning for keywords.

[9:38] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **The more schools teach computers, the less competent kids are with them** — Take the ICILS international digital-literacy test across the decade from 2013 to 2023: the share of children explicitly taught at school how to use a computer rose by about 600%, while the share clearing the minimum digital-literacy threshold fell by about 11%. It holds in every single country — the more technology is emphasized, the less fluent children are with technology. What matters is not whether you can operate the tool but whether you have anything to bring to it; a hammer only means something in the hands of a carpenter.

[12:47] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **An expert offloads to a tool; a child outsources to it** — When an expert uses a tool, that is offloading: he already has enough knowledge to check the output. A statistician would need four hours by hand and the computer returns the result in twenty seconds, but he can tell immediately whether it is right or wrong. When a child uses the same tool, it is outsourcing: he can only type in, copy, and paste, with no idea of the process and no idea whether the result is any good, so all he can do is wait for someone else to nod. The consequence is that he never learns the facts or the procedure — he only learns to depend on the machine.

[22:02] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **Personalized learning only works on material the student already knows** — Individualized practice works only for drilling material already learned, and that is the single place technology is supported by the data. But most of classroom time is spent on things students cannot yet do, and that requires self-regulated learning ability — which about 95% of children do not have. Those children need a teacher giving everyone the same information and a group discussion around it. The data in fact show that once instruction becomes genuinely personalized, most children check out. The irony is that technology was originally sold as the thing that would kill rote memorization, and the one function that works is drill-and-kill.

[27:18] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **AI's errors drift, which is why they never get caught** — AI will accelerate the cognitive decline. An ordinary piece of digital courseware may contain errors, but those errors are fixed, so a teacher can spot and correct them. AI's errors drift, moving anywhere between 20% and 35% at any moment: ten children work the same problem, nine get it right and one gets it wrong, and it is never caught. Someone asked him about the line that ‘the people who can use AI will replace you’; Jared's point is that it is experts who use AI. AI literacy, at bottom, means you have to understand more than the AI does in order to fix the mistakes it makes.

[29:25] (Jared Cooney Horvath) **The fix is not a new system but a return to 2010** — Policy is turning: at the start of the year 3 U.S. states had education-technology bills, and today 31 states do. The Australian state of Victoria has already banned its use for children in year two and below and pulled it back sharply in primary school. The good news, Jared says, is that we do not have to invent a new system — we only have to step back onto the track that already existed in 2010: textbooks, paper and pencil, blackboards, and discussion are all still there. His concrete advice to parents is to buy a printer, keep home study on paper as much as possible, and start talking to teachers about ‘non-essential technology out’.

### verbatim quotes

[1:56] Jared Cooney Horvath: "So we've got this mistaken assumption that technology equals learning."

[12:47] Jared Cooney Horvath: "Now, when you give that exact same tool to a novice to a kid. They are not doing offloading. They're doing what's called outsourcing."

[12:47] Jared Cooney Horvath: "The best they can do is type things into a tool. When it spits it out, they can copy, paste it handed to somebody else."

[28:22] Jared Cooney Horvath: "As soon as you inject AI, they work worse. … the AI just starts to confuse the system more than solidify it."

[29:25] Jared Cooney Horvath: "if you've been in a classroom longer than 10 years, you already know the problem. It's just no one has put words to it yet."

[30:26] Jared Cooney Horvath: "you never asked to have a screen shoved in your face for six hours a day"

### figures

- Hours a year children spend multitasking on computers: more than 2,500 hours [6:09]
- Average interval before distraction when studying on a computer at home: about 6 minutes [6:09]
- Time per classroom hour spent off-task or multitasking: 24-38 minutes [6:09]

- Rise in the share of students explicitly taught digital technology, 2013-2023: about 600% [9:38]

- Grades where the Australian state of Victoria restricts classroom technology: year two and below [29:25]

### glossary

- Ed tech: The connected teaching devices, software, and online tutoring systems used in classrooms.
- ICILS: The International Computer and Information Literacy Study, an international test of students' digital skills, administered once in 2013 and once in 2023.
- Offloading: An expert using a tool to save effort, but with enough knowledge to verify the output himself.
- Outsourcing: A novice handing the thinking and the learning process to a tool, unable to judge whether the result is right.
- SRLs: Self-regulated learning skills — a student's ability to plan, monitor, and adjust their own learning.
- Drill-and-kill: Teaching by heavy repetitive practice until the material is drilled in; usually said with disapproval.

who it is for: K-12 school administrators, parents agonizing over their kids' screen time, education-app founders, and engineers who need to explain to a school why they oppose AI in the classroom.
what to skip: Listeners who only want the what-to-do can jump to the policy and parenting advice after 29:25; the mechanism argument before that can be skipped.

**A run of British government misjudgements in the early 1970s — the Falls Curfew, the refusal to send more troops, indiscriminate internment — turned the Provisional IRA from a fringe armed group into the central actor of a thirty-year conflict, and radicalised British soldiers along the way.**

why listen: The episode reconstructs the psychology of escalating violence through a wealth of first-hand testimony. Worth your time if you want to understand how government decisions can accidentally feed extremism. Dense throughout, with no obvious filler.

### points

[11:08] (Tom) **The Provisional IRA was born of a split over strategy, not community defence** — At a secret meeting in Belfast in December 1969, a group of veteran IRA members unhappy with the movement's Marxist leadership joined forces with younger radicals and decided to break away, founding the Provisional IRA. They argued for achieving a united Ireland by force, parting ways with the Official IRA and its case for political struggle. The armed wing rose fast in the early 1970s and became the central actor in the thirty years of conflict that followed. What is worth noting is that it was not a spontaneous neighbourhood defence organisation but a group of veterans with explicit political aims and years of armed experience, actively choosing the path of violence.

[14:32] (Tom) **Civilian deaths were a price the founders had already calculated** — Tom insists that the Provisional IRA cannot be described as a defensive organisation. Its founding leaders — Mac Stíofáin, Brady and others — were long-standing IRA members with years of struggle behind them, explicitly committed to unification through violence, and openly acknowledged that this would cause civilian casualties while holding that the price was worth paying. This account breaks the narrative popular at the time that the IRA was forced into resistance, and it explains why any government crackdown only strengthened the organisation's legitimacy: it had already decided to fight.

[22:08] (Tom) **The curfew and house searches did the IRA's recruiting for it** — In June 1970 the newly installed prime minister, Heath, decided not to ban the Orange Order parades — a choice one British official called the worst misjudgement he had seen in his life. Violence duly broke out, and the Provisional IRA made its first appearance. On 3 July the British Army imposed a curfew and large-scale house searches on the Falls area of Belfast; weapons were seized, but the brutality of the operation sharpened the community's hostility and delivered a flood of new recruits to the IRA. This became the turning point in the escalation of the conflict: in the name of maintaining order, the Army in effect completed the insurgency's recruitment campaign.

[33:04] (Tom) **Most Britons wanted withdrawal; Heath preferred to let soldiers die** — In February 1971 the IRA member Billy Reid shot dead Robert Curtis, a 20-year-old British soldier, with a Sterling submachine gun — the first British soldier killed in the Troubles. Curtis left a pregnant wife, and his father said he did not know what his son had died for. Polling showed that most people in Britain supported withdrawal, but Heath's cabinet judged that pulling out would bring international condemnation and sectarian slaughter, and refused. The decision let the situation slide further into the abyss, and it pinned the British government to a position of preferring dead soldiers to a political settlement.

[40:29] (Tom) **Escalation did not come only from the IRA; British soldiers were radicalised too** — A Scottish working-class Catholic soldier describes in his memoir the silence that fell over the barracks as news of these killings came in. He looked at the faces of the veterans around him and read the same emotion in all of them: wait until it's our turn. This marks the point at which the British Army, too, began to radicalise. That mood created pressure on the British government: rank-and-file anger would translate into action, which would in turn provoke the IRA further, producing a spiral of violence. Tom uses this first-hand account to show that the escalation was not driven by the IRA alone — the psychological shift inside the Army mattered just as much.

[46:53] (Dominic) **The biggest killer was not the loyalist militias but the IRA** — The Ulster Defence Association (UDA), founded in the autumn of 1971, was the largest loyalist self-defence organisation, with 25,000 to 40,000 members at its peak and a women's unit as well. Over the course of the conflict the UDA committed more than 400 murders, almost all of Catholic civilians. But Dominic points out that the IRA killed far more people than that, making it the single biggest killer of the entire conflict. The point breaks the simple narrative that the IRA was the only violent party, and it shows that the Troubles were a two-way sectarian war rather than a straightforward anti-colonial struggle.

[1:05:00] (Dominic) **Arresting only Catholics amounted to recruiting for the IRA** — Operation Demetrius arrested 342 people, all of them Catholics and not one a Protestant. Maudling later argued that a Protestant organisation behaving as the IRA did would have been treated the same way, but the fact was that the UVF had already begun killing. Because the intelligence behind the operation was out of date, it arrested the wrong people and made the conflict worse. Dominic notes that such a blatant imbalance made the Catholic community feel systematically discriminated against, and became the best recruiting advertisement the IRA could have had. Internment was a failure both militarily and morally, and it drove the violence straight onward.

## Mental events follow no laws, yet reasons can still be causes that leave us free

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-pel-心物无规律-理由仍可作为原因而自由/
- show: The Partially Examined Life (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/pel/)
- original episode: Ep. 398: Donald Davidson on Mind vs. Body (Part Two)
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 53:45
- transcript: Machine transcription · 10209 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 3 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Davidson argues that mental events fall under no strict laws and are identical to physical events only as particulars; but in the explanation of action, reasons are genuinely causes, and when a reason causes an action the agent is precisely then free.**

why listen: Two complementary papers expose the most awkward joint in the physicalist framework; the argument is dense and the objections have to be taken apart one by one, but that is exactly where the payoff is.

### points

[2:20] **Reducing belief to behavior collapses into an infinite regress** — Davidson points out that reducing beliefs and desires to behavior — defining belief, for instance, as assenting to a proposition — collapses into an infinite regress: to judge whether a given act of assent is genuine assent, you have to appeal to a further intention, and every layer requires a new condition. Beliefs and desires therefore have content only inside a whole made up of other beliefs and desires. This holism in the mental domain establishes both that the mental is autonomous and that it lacks the kind of lawlikeness the physical domain has, which is what grounds the claim that the mental is anomalous.

[8:11] **Between the mental and the physical there are correlations, never laws** — Homonomic generalizations stay inside one and the same conceptual scheme — length measurement, say, built out of a set of postulates and axioms applied to macroscopic objects, and refinable step by step toward a strict law. Heteronomic generalizations instead link physical vocabulary to mental vocabulary. Davidson holds that cross-domain generalizations of this kind cannot be tightened into laws by adding further conditions, because describing the correlation necessarily means switching into the other vocabulary. So between the mental and the physical there are only loose correlations, no strict laws — and that is the core of anomalous monism.

[15:52] **If the mental is to cause movement, it must be a physical event** — Davidson establishes the identity of mental and physical events in three steps: suppose a mental event M causes a physical event P; then under some description M and P must fall under a strict law; and the only strict law available is a physical law. So M falls under a physical law, which means M has a physical description — M is itself a physical event. Refusing this identity leaves only a retreat to Cartesian interactionism, with mental substances intruding on the closed circuit of physical causation for no reason at all. A variant of Laplace's demon is used to reinforce the conclusion: knowing every physical fact still gets you to no mental event whatsoever.

[23:31] **Wanting the light on is not wanting my arm to move just so** — Davidson uses the light-switch example to pull apart the object of an intention: wanting to turn the light on is not the same as wanting my arm to travel along one precise path; every detail of what actually happens (angle, speed, timing) is a contingent token. As he writes, the details of the action are of course all fixed, but it makes no sense to demand that my wanting be aimed at one unique moment or manner of acting. The point answers behaviorism and volitionism at once: no surplus ghost of the will needs to be introduced, because a general pro attitude plus a belief already explains why this particular token action occurred on this occasion.

[31:49] **Whether physical causation is really closed is not obvious** — If one and the same event has several mental descriptions (wanting to signal, wanting to turn on the light, wanting to light up the room) and also several layers of physical description (molecules, cells, muscles), then which physical event does token-token identity match the mental event to? Davidson gives no answer. Participants note that the language games of the biological and the physical levels are likewise irreducible to each other, and may even involve emergence between levels; which means it is not obvious that the closed circuit of physical causation is genuinely closed. This is one of the few places in the episode the author never defends, and the largest doubt the discussion leaves standing.

[38:11] **When an action succeeds, the act of will is a redundant step** — Host Mark offers one way to read it: separate the mental state that corresponds to the reason from the mental state of resolving to act, give each its own brain state, and let the brain states form a physical causal chain; then "reasons are causes" becomes: the reason, as a physical event, causes bodily movement by way of the physical correlate of the volition. The Wittgensteinian objection is that an extra mental event of willing is needed only in cases where the will fails (paralysis, for instance); adding it in the successful case is redundant. The disagreement exposes that the levels of reason, intention and causation in Davidson's text are not fully sorted out.

[44:42] **The plate broke because of a hidden crack: states can be causes too** — The first objection: beliefs and desires are only states or dispositions, causes must be events, so states are not causes. Davidson replies that we are perfectly willing to say "my head hit the door frame because I am tall" or "the plate broke because it had a hidden crack" — states and structures can do causal work. More importantly, mental states such as perception are not static dispositions; they change over time, they are dynamic. So there is no reason to insist that only events can enter causal explanation; states can too, as long as they sit at the right place in the physical causal chain.

[50:00] **Only when reasons are causes is the agent a willing agent** — The sharpest objection is that attributing an action to a cause turns the person into a victim of physical necessity. Davidson turns the question around: why should having a cause turn an action into a mere happening and the person into a victim? It is when a reason causes an action that the agent is a willing agent. Granting that reasons are causes does not erase agency; on the contrary, only by making reasons causal factors that bring actions about can a person act meaningfully in the physical world, rather than being reduced to a shell that gets redescribed after the fact. This is the heart of his answer to the worry about free will.

### verbatim quotes

[2:20] : "beliefs and desires issue in behavior only as modified and mediated by further beliefs and desires, attitudes and attendings without limit."

[5:44] : "mental and physical predicates are not a priori made for one another"

[14:50] : "There cannot be tight connection. Between the realms, if each is to retain its allegiance to its proper sorts of evidence."

[23:31] : "Every detail is fixed, but it makes no sense to demand that my want be directed at an action performed at any one moment or done in the same unique manner"

[50:00] : "why on earth should a cause turn an action into a mere happening and a person into it help as a victim"

### figures

- Publication years of the two papers: Mental Events: 1970; Actions, Reasons and Causes: 1963 [0:00]
- Length of the appendix to Davidson's paper: 3 pages [6:57]
- Pages left undiscussed: 8 pages [43:38]

### glossary

- token identity: Mental and physical events are one and the same event as concrete particulars, not a lawlike correspondence between types.
- homonomic generalization: A generalization within a single vocabulary that can be refined toward a strict law, as in length measurement.
- heteronomic generalization: A generalization spanning mental and physical vocabulary that cannot be refined into a law.
- pro attitude: Covers desires, wants, principles — every inclination that pushes toward action.
- primary reason: A pro attitude plus the relevant belief, together constituting the complete causal explanation of an action.
- rationalization: Describing an action as having a reason, that is, clothing it in an intentional description.

who it is for: Readers in philosophy and cognitive science who want to work out why reasons can be causes, and how anomalous monism squares with freedom; product people and researchers curious about physicalist accounts of mind and body.
tags: Mind-body problem, Philosophy of action, Anomalous monism, Causal explanation, Davidson, Analytic philosophy

## A 22-Year-Old CEO, Five Rounds, Over $100 Million: The First Term Sheet Decides Everything

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-crossing-具身创业最优解-快融资-软条款-全栈开源/
- show: 十字路口Crossing (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/crossing/)
- original episode: 22 岁的具身 CEO、5 轮融资、过亿美元、“不知天有多高”、“一年吃了十年的苦”｜对谈黄一：萝博派对创始人/CEO
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 1:02:53
- transcript: Machine transcription · 20874 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 2 quotes matched verbatim, 9 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In a year and a half, 22-year-old Huang Yi has grown RoboParty to nearly 150 people: five rounds totalling over $100 million, and RPO shipping around 100 units a month. His calls: the first round's terms decide whether you live or die, open source is a moat because it lowers the friction of working with you, and the robot body is the entry point to embodied AI.**

why listen: Everything here is hands-on, dug out of five rounds of fundraising: how to pick an FA, how to negotiate a TS, what a round-every-two-months cadence feels like, plus how open source turns into a moat and how you run 150 people. No abstractions.

### points

[3:00] (Huang Yi) **What you should fear is not a board seat but personal liability** — At the seed round you want as many cards in hand as you can get, but what matters more are the terms of that first agreement — they will carry over essentially unchanged all the way to Pre-IPO. Huang Yi stresses that the company still has no redemption rights and no VAM clauses, and that this comes down to negotiating the first round on friendly enough terms. He is not afraid of giving up a board seat: as long as the shareholder genuinely helps (Xiaomi, for instance), handing over a seat actually makes the collaboration run smoother. What you really have to guard against are the buried traps — personal joint liability, redemption with simple or compound interest — which is why you must find a lawyer who has negotiated a large volume of investment terms.

[7:07] (Huang Yi) **Don't dodge the bubble; it is the industry's momentum** — Huang Yi flatly concedes ‘of course there's a bubble’, but he treats the bubble as the industry's momentum: suppliers give you a second look because you are in embodied AI, and talent pours in from other sectors. Shunwei taught him to ride the trend — no company can change its era, you can only build your company while the heat is on; the counterexamples are photovoltaics and real estate, where nobody is looking. He also explains where the money comes from: the secondary market has capital, another bag of money becomes an LP inside a GP, and that turns into ammunition for startups. The sentiment cycle is the fundraising window.

[12:14] (Huang Yi) **Take everything you can raise, but not every check is worth taking** — RoboParty closes a round every one to two months, which looks insane, but behind it sits a clear set of milestones: shipping the RP1 launch plus volume production is the Series A bar, and closing the commercial loop is the Series B bar. Huang Yi's logic is that on the industry's way up you take as much as you can take, because missing the window may cost you another year of waiting. But he also insists that not all money should be taken: dollar funds weigh technical leadership, RMB funds care more about commercialization, and the later the stage, the less professional the investors he tends to run into.

[21:22] (Huang Yi) **The value isn't the robot body, it's the empty layer between model and body** — Asked ‘how do you make money if the whole stack is open source’, Huang Yi offers two concepts: a threshold is how much fixed assets and headcount you put in, while a moat is where the money is. He positions RoboParty in the missing layer between the model companies and the vendors that have commercial robot bodies — the model companies have no body, and existing body makers won't open up the low levels, so the motor layer, URDF snapshots and data-collection interfaces are all absent. Open source lowers the friction of working with you and widens the brand; selling bodies is the base business, but the compounding from users is bigger: one CMU professor buying a body effectively brings in two PhD engineers at million-level annual salaries who keep publishing papers.

[37:38] (Huang Yi) **The honeycomb only suits the Lab; manufacturing has to have process** — A company of nearly 150 people runs on a ‘honeycomb structure’: each person has at most six effective connection surfaces, driven by talent density rather than hierarchy — an idea taken from Anthropic. But Huang Yi says plainly that the honeycomb only suits the Lab; if the whole-machine division also went talent-driven, you get the chaos of ‘nobody even knows who to buy parts from’. So the company carves out a pure Lab that runs on honeycomb logic, while the manufacturing division must have process, and the two sides absorb each other's knowhow through a communication-style meeting system.

[46:43] (Huang Yi) **Embodied gross margins are double the carmakers', so the giants will come** — Huang Yi offers a read on the landscape: there are roughly 300 embodied companies today, and by 2030 perhaps only 10 to 15 will make it into the next round. He uses gross margin as the yardstick: embodied runs around 40% while carmakers are at only 20%, so the next wave of players will be companies at the hundreds-of-billions scale — NIO, XPeng and Li Auto, Honor, Geely. Only when BYD, Huawei, CATL, BAT and Xiaomi finally step in does ‘the big era’ truly begin. He is also bullish on model companies like OpenAI and Zhipu, arguing that once they fill in their robotics understanding, their scaling ability far exceeds a startup's.

[55:45] (Huang Yi) **China doesn't reward explorers, it rewards the people who pull it off** — Asked which embodied companies in China and the US he admires most, Huang Yi names Tesla, Figure, and Shuran Song's team Generalyst — the ones willing to explore paradigms nobody has attempted, which in the US is what attracts the most money. But he says outright that Chinese culture does not reward the explorer; it rewards the person who ‘can get a company off the ground’. He has deliberately chosen the second path, and he gives an extremely concrete standard for success: that his parents, without knowing he built this robot, would be willing to buy one and take it home.

[1:01:51] (Huang Yi) **The body is halfway through; the brain doesn't even know where the finish is** — Using a marathon as the metaphor for embodied progress, Huang Yi splits it into segments: the body is already at the halfway mark, with iteration and convergence left; the cerebellum (whole-body coordination) is also about halfway, and the behavior foundation model can already handle interactions like ‘carrying something back to its original position’. On the brain he is most candid — ‘I don't know what number it is’ — because nobody has seen the endgame. He thinks the endgame is ‘an agent that has accumulated your entire history and reacts exactly the way you would’, and by that definition we have run only one or two kilometers today. This is the one place in the whole conversation where he admits a gap in his own understanding.

## What Etched's chip really solves may be bandwidth, not compute

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-techtechpotato-etched的芯片-可能解决的是带宽而不是算力/
- show: TechTechPotato (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/techtechpotato/)
- original episode: The Reason My Phone is Ringing Daily: Etched
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: —
- transcript: YouTube captions · 2341 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Etched welds the transformer into hardware with 0.45-volt ultra-low-voltage transistors and direct cross-chip SRAM access, but the host suspects the problem actually being solved is bandwidth, not compute.**

why listen: Two technologies that had previously been announced by name only, with no explanation of how they work, are taken apart and explained for the first time — but chip power draw, bandwidth, the compiler and customer volume are all still unanswered. Information density is moderate to high.

### points

[1:04] **The founder himself admits this chip may turn out to be wasted work** — Two years ago Etched went public with a position: build a chip just for transformers. The transformer was already the mainstream architecture for language models at that point, but it was still a very specific type of workload. The public argument was that a chip built only for transformers can run both fast and cheap, at the cost that once the technical direction shifts, the chip may be worthless. The CEO admits himself that if the market turns, everything they have done may have been for nothing. This is a bet whose risk of failure was publicly acknowledged from the very beginning.

[2:05] **A 23-year-old dropout plus chip veterans is what unlocked the big rounds** — CEO Gavin Uberti is a 23-year-old dropout from Harvard's computer science department. Co-founder Robert Wacken also came out of Harvard, but from the university's tech-transfer side, helping companies get from zero to funded. CTO Mark Ross has Cisco and Cypress Semi on his record; his LinkedIn says he led the team that built the first multi-port Ethernet switch on the market, and he also worked on Soho-related technology. The combination of young founders and seasoned chip veterans is part of why this company has been able to raise such large rounds.

[3:05] **A reporter's site visit turned up blinking lights, not silicon** — When the company first appeared it claimed a chassis of eight chips could take on Nvidia, saying it could reach 500,000 tokens per second — many times the figure Nvidia was advertising at the time. Around the same period, EE Times reporter Sally visited the headquarters in person and saw a pile of servers blinking and beeping, but never actually saw the silicon itself. It took more than a year before the company really came out of stealth and the chip taped out, so what Sally saw at the time was in all likelihood only a test chip.

[5:07] **Low voltage buys more compute units, at the cost of clock frequency** — An ordinary high-end desktop CPU runs at roughly 1.2 to 1.3 volts, and even the most efficient desktop and laptop processors sit in the range close to 1 volt. etched's low-voltage inference chip runs at about 450 millivolts, that is 0.45 volts, already approaching the threshold voltage at which a transistor can just barely switch. The lower the voltage, the more you can multiply the number of compute units you pack in; the price is that frequency cannot go high. The only high-compute industry currently using ultra-low-voltage transistors like this at scale is Bitcoin mining rigs, because mining algorithms need only a tiny amount of data moving in and out, whereas machine learning is precisely a workload of hauling data back and forth — which is exactly the next problem etched has to solve.

[8:13] **Cache should not belong only to the chip that holds it** — etched's chip has HBM inside the package, and inside the chip a large block of SRAM cache (scratch pad) shared by all the compute units on-die. The second technology, cluster scale memory, opens that SRAM cache up to other chips for direct access over a high-speed interconnect — something like RDMA across chips, directly reading and writing another chip's cache and scratch pad rather than using it only inside the chip. High-speed interconnect needs voltage, so the power saved by low-voltage compute may be shifted over to feeding this cross-chip communication.

[9:15] **A chassis full of black cables reveals where the power budget goes** — In the photos etched showed of the physical server, the first thing that draws the eye is the dense mass of black cabling, visibly far more than in Nvidia's or AMD's systems. Some of the cables are for liquid cooling, but a large share is believed to be for high-bandwidth interconnect like cluster scale memory. From this the host infers that what etched really solves may not be a compute problem but the bandwidth problem of chip-to-chip communication — the power headroom saved by low-voltage compute gets spent piling up interconnect bandwidth.

[10:18] **Hard-coded does not mean frozen; the chip is still programmable** — Neither of the two technology names — low-voltage inference and cluster scale memory — mentions transformers, which suggests the real binding happens in the physical arrangement of the compute units: this is a chip hard-coded for the transformer, but still programmable, able to run different versions of the transformer, unlike the other special-purpose chip design reported on a few weeks ago, which was rigid. The host has not yet had the chance to go through the details with the team on how transcendental functions get computed, how memory addresses are managed, and how data moving in and out of the scratch pad is tracked — if all of that falls back on the compiler, then you have to hope their compiler is genuinely good.

[12:19] **Before selling a million chips, first prove you can sell a thousand** — etched says it already has plenty of interest from hyperscale cloud providers, but the host cites Jim Keller's line: if you want to sell a million chips, you first have to prove you can sell a hundred thousand; to sell a hundred thousand, you first have to prove ten thousand; to sell ten thousand, you first have to prove a thousand — the question a startup should really be asked is always where your hundred-unit, thousand-unit and ten-thousand-unit customers are. Co-founder Robert Wacken said at a funding event that etched's internal core tenet is ‘delivery’, meaning getting the chip built a year earlier than other startups founded around the same time, and that they intend to keep up this fast iteration pace as much as possible in bringing out the next generation of chips.

### glossary

- tape out: The final step after a chip design is frozen: sending it to the fab for full production manufacturing.
- RDMA: Remote direct memory access: reading and writing another device's memory or cache directly, bypassing its CPU.
- threshold voltage: The minimum voltage needed for a transistor to just barely turn on (conduct).
- cluster scale memory: A technology proposed by etched that lets multiple chips share each other's SRAM cache over a high-speed interconnect.

who it is for: Investors and chip engineers following non-Nvidia AI chip startups, compute efficiency and bandwidth bottlenecks, who want to know whether transformer-specific chips have anything real behind the funding hype.
what to skip: The closing stretch where the host pitches his own merch store can be skipped; it contains no information.

## The moat in evals is not the AI — it is human taste

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-peteryang-自下而上的评估-是-ai-给不了你的护城河/
- show: Peter Yang (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/peteryang/)
- original episode: How to Build Better AI Evals with Claude Code in 5 Steps | Shreya & Hamel
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 54:20
- transcript: YouTube captions · 10288 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**You cannot leave eval design to the AI: it is good at top-down criteria, but the bottom-up evals that actually decide whether a product is good — the taste distilled out of error data — have to come from a human, and only then get executed at scale with Claude Code.**

why listen: No hand-waving. A 15-minute live demo turns ‘finding your errors’ into an actual workflow, plus benchmark numbers on the automated eval tools. The second half, on how precise those tools really are, is the most valuable part.

### points

[6:03] (Shreya) **The model can write your criteria, but never your taste** — Shreya splits evals into two kinds. Top-down criteria are set in advance from the nature of the task itself — length, actionability. Bottom-up criteria come out of browsing a large volume of samples and hardening a vague, intuitive dissatisfaction into a rule. Claude is very good at the top-down half, but the bottom-up half has to be supplied by a human, because the model has no way of knowing your taste out of thin air. That is also why evals have to be iterative: every new failure mode you find adds another criterion — though be careful not to overfit to a single interview.

[9:05] (Shreya) **Hand a judge too long a rubric and it will quietly skip criteria** — Shreya suggests splitting your criteria into two groups and having subagents grade each group separately, so the model does not get lazy and ignore items when facing one long checklist. She also has the skill auto-generate a spreadsheet (or pivot table) laying out pass and fail for every criterion, which lets you see quickly which criteria matter more for the task in front of you — and even weight them by hand, instead of deferring blindly to uniform weights.

[17:08] (Shreya) **Fifteen minutes building an interface beats squinting at a spreadsheet** — Shreya demoed her error discovery skill. Step one: read the data and work out its semantic type — is this an article, code, or a trace? Step two: design the visual encoding, using color, spacing and opacity to make differences in the data pop so a human can actually see them. Step three: build the review interface with HTML and Python. Step four: let the AI cluster the data and pick out a diverse set of samples. Step five: enter the interaction loop — you leave open-ended feedback in the interface, and Claude Code reads it in real time and folds it back into new samples or new eval criteria. The whole flow takes about 15 minutes, and what you buy is readability far beyond what a table gives you.

[27:19] (Hamel) **Humans only have to say what they dislike; let the AI do the sorting** — Hamel explains the machinery behind that loop. As a person reads samples, they drop open-ended comments in passing — ‘I don't like the negative contrast’, ‘this is annoying but I can't say why’ — and a Claude monitor tool running in the background keeps digesting those comments. Once roughly ten have accumulated it starts inducing themes on its own, then proactively sweeps the full sample set and labels every instance of the same problem. The core philosophy: humans supply taste and judgment, the AI supplies discovery and categorization at scale, rather than inventing the criteria for you.

[35:23] (Shreya) **What error analysis produces is your eval rubric itself** — Shreya points out that error analysis yields more than a list of problems — those failure modes convert directly into your rubric, which is to say your eval criteria. Of the 361 suggestions auto-generated in her demo, the most common were staccato fragments of fewer than four words (249 of them). Write those criteria into the skill and every future generation can be judged against them item by item with an LLM judge. And because you already have a human-labeled dataset, you can run the check in reverse and validate whether the eval criteria themselves are reliable.

[44:28] (Hamel) **What automated eval tools miss is exactly the product judgment** — Hamel shared their benchmarking of automated eval tools like Brain Trust, Arize and LangSmith: they catch the obvious failures — tool calls that fail, users expressing dissatisfaction — but they broadly miss the implicit errors that require product judgment. Take a real estate sales bot facing the objection ‘you don't have this listing’: it will only say ‘sorry, we don't’, and never propose an alternative. More notable still: coding agents like Claude Code and Codex perform the same as those tools, because the underlying models and prompts are essentially the same.

[50:33] (Shreya) **Even 90% precision is not enough — false positives skew your direction** — Shreya adds that automated eval tools top out at 80%-90% precision even in the best case, which means 10%-20% of the errors they flag are false positives, and acting on them blindly will skew your product direction. So the approach that actually works is: use the tools to find the obvious errors fast, then review the data by hand — validating what the tools found, filling in what they missed, and making sure your taste gets injected into the product. That is what opens a gap between you and your competitors.

[52:35] (Shreya) **Trade evals for a cheaper model and cut cost by 100x** — On the depth of the course, Shreya says that beyond error analysis and productionizing, it also covers wiring evals into CI/CD, monitoring long-term drift, and adversarial evals (guarding against tenant data leakage). The most practical part is the improvement module: using evals to guide a model switch — when you move to a cheaper model, you use evals to optimize its accuracy, and they have in practice cut costs for students and clients by 100x. That is an engineering capability on top of pure eval skill.

## Ebola infects neurons and keeps shedding virus for 120 days; a fish cancer spreads between fish

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-twiv-埃博拉持续感染脑神经元-鱼类黑色素瘤能传染/
- show: This Week in Virology (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/twiv/)
- original episode: TWiV 1351: Ebola Virus Brains and Contagious Catfish Cancers
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 1:41:09
- transcript: Machine transcription · 15662 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Brain organoids show that Ebola can infect neurons and keep releasing infectious virus for 120 days; melanomas in a brown bullhead population descend from a single clonal ancestor and spread from fish to fish. The boundaries of viral persistence and of transmissible cancer get rewritten at the same time.**

why listen: This episode delivers two evidence chains that can change how you understand mechanism: Ebola's long-term persistence in brain organoids, and the clonal lineage behind a transmissible melanoma. The transmissible-cancer segment is dense with phylogenetic and shared-SNV data, and rewards close reading.

### points

[8:13] (Rich Condit) **Three-tier scoring gives political appointees more room to pick projects** — NIH has proposed replacing the numerical scores in grant review with three tiers — good, medium, poor — on the grounds that the current numbers are severely compressed, with large numbers of grants bunched at nearly the same score and very little discrimination between them; the three-tier system is already in use at NSF. Rich does not object to tiering as such, but he says the real problem is that all three of them now distrust NIH's leadership: vague tiers make it easier for political appointees to select projects on ideological grounds. He also recalls that NSF gave him partial funding back when his first grant was rejected.

[22:34] (Alan Dove) **Detecting RNA is not persistence; what counts is whether virus is released** — A team at the Bernhard Nocht Institute in Hamburg used human brain organoids to study Ebola's long-term persistence, and drew a distinction between two kinds of persistence: productive persistence, the continued release of infectious particles, and nonproductive persistence, where only RNA can be detected. microglia at MOI 1 or 10 remained persistently infected through 13 passages over 91 days; across the organoid as a whole the infection rate exceeded 90%, with virus produced continuously for 120 days. Once the definition is made explicit, ‘persistent infection’ can no longer be waved through on an RT-PCR positive alone — you have to show that complete virus is being released.

[37:55] (Alan Dove) **Ebola infects neurons directly, which had never been reported before** — The team watched infection spread through the organoid: the virus advanced from the periphery toward the center, infecting neurons, astrocytes and microglia. Neuronal infection had never been reported before, which rewrites the earlier view that Ebola is not neurotropic. microglia clustered around the infected cells, suggesting that innate immunity was attempting a response; Lassa virus, used as a control, disappeared from the organoids within 48 days, while Ebola was still there. The difference suggests that replication in the brain is not incidental contamination.

[45:04] **The immune response both attacks and brakes, which helps the virus linger** — What happens in an infected organoid is not simply destructive inflammation. The researchers detected pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and anti-inflammatory mediators simultaneously in the infected brain organoids. This says that the host's inflammatory response is a self-balancing system, with an attack and a brake. For a persisting virus, a moderately suppressed immune environment is more favorable to long-term coexistence than a one-sided inflammatory storm.

[49:08] **The mutations found in organoids have never been seen in survivors** — The authors acknowledge that the model is isolated from the in vivo environment and lacks contributors to immune-privileged status such as the blood-brain barrier; more importantly, the single-nucleotide variants that arise in the organoids have never been reported in survivors of Ebola virus disease, which points to a fundamental difference between the two. Many of the mutations are thought to reduce or block viral replication, and low-level replication may in fact be what allows the virus to maintain itself within the cell population. Persistence need not rest on high titer; it may rest on replication low enough not to trigger clearance.

[51:16] **Pollution is not the culprit: this cancer spreads between fish** — Since 2012, fishermen on Lake Memphremagog (between Maine and Quebec) have repeatedly caught brown bullhead (Amiurus nebulosus) bearing raised black lesions, identified histologically as malignant melanoma. In sampling between 2014 and 2017, 23%–37% of the fish carried lesions. Suspicion initially fell on runoff pollution from Tropical Storm Irene in 2011 as the trigger, but the later data pointed in a rarer direction — the tumor itself can spread from fish to fish. The lake has become a natural site for observing how a cancer becomes a pathogen.

[1:00:43] **The lake's tumors all descend from one clone, and it came from elsewhere** — Two genomic analyses corroborate each other. On the mitochondrial genome tree, all the tumor samples form a single monophyletic group, meaning they descend from a single ancestor; and the tumor sequences resemble neither the normal tissue of the same fish nor the normal tissue of other fish in the lake, whose sequences scatter across the tree. Single-nucleotide variant analysis of the nuclear genome likewise yields a monophyletic group, and these tumor genomes are closer to unaffected reference fish from New Hampshire and Maine than to the other fish in the lake — so the clone driving the transmission did not originate in this lake, but was introduced from somewhere else.

[1:03:54] **Human cancer mutations are each distinct; over half of these fish mutations are shared** — The harder evidence comes from variant-sharing statistics. Across 16 tumor–normal tissue pairs, 245,000 tumor-specific SNVs and 61,000 brain-specific SNVs were identified; 59% of the tumor-specific SNVs are shared by at least 14 fish, whereas 83% of the brain-tissue-specific SNVs occur in only one fish. For comparison, in human melanoma databases 94% of SNVs are unique to a single cancer, and only 0.008% are shared by more than 10 cancers. Such a high proportion of shared variants in the fish tumors, the paper's authors argue, further supports the conclusion that these cancers come from the same clone and are transmissible.

## Terror birds weren't killed by humans — the Isthmus of Panama closed first

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-23-ancients-恐怖鸟死于物种大交换而非人类/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: Terror Birds
- published: 2026-08-23 · duration: 45:14
- transcript: Machine transcription · 8870 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Terror birds were the apex avian predators that emerged on the island continent of South America after the dinosaurs died out, and they ruled for tens of millions of years; their eventual disappearance is tied to the great species interchange that followed the joining of the Isthmus of Panama, earlier than the arrival of humans in South America.**

why listen: The value here is in the mechanisms rather than the names: the trade of flight for body size, the weaponized skull, and the extinction timeline each come with a chain of evidence. Where the early evidence is thin, the speaker keeps modeled inference separate from what is confirmed.

### points

[4:04] (Steve) **The first fossil was filed as a relative of the anteater** — In the 19th century the Ameghino brothers in Argentina were the first to find the animal, and all they had was a toothless piece of jawbone a few inches long. They took it for the lower jaw of a mammal whose teeth had dropped out during fossilization, and so placed it with the group containing anteaters, sloths and armadillos. Only later did it become clear that the jaw had no teeth because it was never a tooth-bearing jaw at all — it was part of a beak. That early confusion also explains why the nickname "terror bird" caught on more widely than the complicated scientific name.

[6:17] (Steve) **Terror birds were already gone before the first humans reached South America** — The oldest known terror bird fossils come from the Eocene, about 50 to 55 million years ago, but the fossil record is patchy and they may have appeared earlier — possibly getting under way not long after T. rex and Triceratops died out around 66 million years ago. Terror birds went on evolving and diversifying in South America, and the last group of them only vanishes from the fossil record a few tens of thousands of years ago — earlier than the arrival of the first humans in South America. That is why Brusatte is emphatic on the point: the extinction of the terror birds was not the work of humans. This time humans are not to blame.

[8:27] (Steve) **Only a continent cut off from the world could grow terror birds** — For a long stretch after the dinosaurs died out, South America was an "island continent" like Australia today, connected to no other landmass — isolated for perhaps 60 to 90 million years. Gene flow for animals and plants was severed; in a biologist's phrase, everything evolved on its own in "splendid isolation," which is why the continent produced so many strange species found nowhere else. It was inside this ecological fortress that terror birds became the top predators; the cats, bears and dogs of North America had not yet entered South America, so birds held the large-predator niche.

[10:38] (Steve) **Being able to crack seeds was the get-out-of-extinction card after the impact** — 66 million years ago an asteroid about 10 kilometers wide struck near the Yucatán Peninsula in what is now the Gulf of Mexico, with more force than a billion nuclear bombs combined, plunging the world into years of darkness and cold. 75% of species went extinct. The large dinosaurs ate too much, grew too slowly and had a hard time hiding, so they fell first; the birds that survived were small-bodied, fast-growing, able to fly, and equipped with beaks that could eat seeds. With plants dying off en masse, seeds were just about the last food source left, and being able to crack them amounted to a get-out-of-extinction card.

[16:34] (Steve) **Birds are dinosaurs, so the age of dinosaurs never ended** — Once the nuclear winter lifted and sunlight came back through the clouds, the world was barren but full of opportunity. T. rex, Triceratops and the long-necked dinosaurs were gone, and evolution dislikes a vacuum: starting from a handful of survivors, birds and mammals diversified rapidly within a few million years, filling the herbivore, predator and every other niche. The host takes the moment to make the point: this period can still be called the age of dinosaurs, because birds are dinosaurs. Understand that sentence and you understand how terror birds could reach the top of the food chain in South America.

[21:06] (Steve) **Losing flight wasn't decay; it was the trade that bought body size** — The terror birds' closest living relatives are the seriemas; within the first few million years after the dinosaurs died out, birds of this group reached South America, and one lineage gave up flight. That was not degeneration but an evolutionary trade-off: a bird has to beat its wings with muscle, and once body size passes a certain threshold, flying becomes wildly uneconomical. Only by shedding the ability to fly could the body scale up to several hundred kilograms. Elephant birds and the "demon duck" were larger than terror birds, but they ate plants; the accurate title for a terror bird is therefore "largest avian predator," not "largest bird."

[24:25] (Steve) **It didn't bite and tear; it pinned prey down and jabbed repeatedly** — A terror bird's skull was about the size of a horse's head. Birds have no teeth — in fact the embryo does start growing teeth inside the egg, but they are quickly replaced by the beak — and the terror bird's beak carried a large hook, like an eagle's beak enlarged and made sharper. Many of the bones in the skull were fused together, making it sturdier than in most living birds. Paleontologists built biomechanical models with engineering software and found that their bite force was strong, with the skull structure reinforced specifically to withstand that force. Brusatte's image: first pin the prey down with a clawed foot, then jab at it over and over in rhythm, like Muhammad Ali.

[40:26] (Steve) **The land bridge does not mean terror birds lost out to jaguars** — About 2.5 million years ago North and South America were formally joined at the Isthmus of Panama, and the land corridor became a species highway: jaguars, bears and dogs moved south into South America, while opossums, armadillos and others spread north. This great species interchange was an enormous disturbance to South American ecosystems, and terror birds subsequently disappear from the fossil record. Brusatte does not simply put that down to losing a competition; the drastic ice-age climate shifts of the time may also have been at work, or both together. Some terror birds did reach Florida, Texas and California, but failed to establish themselves. The last terror birds went extinct tens of thousands of years before humans arrived in South America.

## Ukrainians Are Fighting the War With Poems and Artifacts, Not Weapons

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-22-iq2-在乌克兰-文化是值得用生命去救的东西/
- show: Intelligence Squared (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/iq2/)
- original episode: Is Ukraine’s Culture Worth Fighting For? With Charlotte Higgins
- published: 2026-08-22 · duration: 37:37
- transcript: Machine transcription · 5759 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 4 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**How the war turned a culture reporter into a language student and prose writers into poets: Ukrainians are resisting the war's erasure of identity and memory by rescuing artifacts and writing poems.**

why listen: Charlotte spent four years going deep into Ukraine and came back with a perspective war reporting rarely offers: culture as the lens for understanding resistance, not as decoration. Having lived it herself makes her conclusions more credible.

### points

[2:20] (Charlotte Higgins) **Culture is not a thing you look at, it is a lens you look through** — After years of writing culture coverage, Charlotte says she grew less and less satisfied with simply judging whether a work was good or bad. She came to see culture as a lens for looking at the world rather than an object put in front of you to look at. The idea took shape gradually over 2020-2021. After the full-scale invasion, a Guardian colleague suggested she cover Ukrainian culture, and she agreed immediately. She believed artists would record this war the way they had recorded the First World War, and that what they left behind would be a deeper and more durable memory than news reporting.

[4:41] (Charlotte Higgins) **The war is not out on a border, it is in the middle of Kyiv** — On her first trip to Kyiv, Russian forces had already been out of the city's surroundings for several months, and away from the front line everything was calm. Then, on the day she arrived, Kyiv was hit by its first large-scale cruise missile attack in months. She calls it a "pretty brutal" awakening. In that moment she understood that this was not a country that merely happened to have fighting on its border: the war had come back into the civilian centre of the city, and from then on that became the norm. Her own experience lets readers feel directly what she was reporting on — the cultural workers who go to work under that threat every day.

[10:00] (Charlotte Higgins) **People turned to poetry because everyday language had stopped being enough** — In his question, the host points out that many people in the book had been writing prose or plays before the war and turned to poetry once it began. Charlotte agrees, and offers two levels of explanation. On the practical level: poems are short, and can be finished on the move, in the moment; a novel by its nature demands time and sitting down. On the deeper level: the shock of the full-scale invasion was so great that everyday language no longer sufficed, and poetry is good at reassembling fragments of meaning. Ukrainian poets told her that in war, poetry falls back to its most elemental forms — laments for the dead, lullabies for children, curses for the enemy.

[13:08] (Charlotte Higgins) **Soldiers starting to write long prose is the sadder news, not the better** — She says that on a recent trip to a literary festival in Kyiv she found large numbers of soldiers writing prose and long memoirs, and that this is in fact a sadder sign. Writing a novel or a book-length work of non-fiction takes time, and the war has now dragged on for four years, so soldiers finally have the time to write something long. The shift in form is a mirror of the war's lengthening, and a sign that it has settled into a sustained, destructive state. Poetry was the immediate reaction; prose is the delayed sediment.

[22:15] (Charlotte Higgins) **Once an object is lost, the past can no longer be read out of it** — She describes a group of young people at a museum in Lviv whose leader, as the front line moved, would rush semi-officially into dangerous areas to rescue artifacts and ask permission afterwards. Charlotte says she found it hard to understand at the time: who would stand in front of a rocket launcher just to rescue a poet's hat and a few personal effects? But the answer is that these people would. Her explanation: what makes you feel you belong to a national community is not only the intangible things like history and language — objects and artifacts are part of it too. Objects can be broken, lost, stolen, and once they are gone no knowledge can ever be drawn from them again. They have to exist for the past to remain legible.

[27:44] (Charlotte Higgins) **The war destroys artifacts and also kills the people documenting them** — Victoria Amelina was a well-known Ukrainian novelist who switched to working as a war crimes investigator after the war began; she died in a missile strike in July 2023, aged only 37. Charlotte recalls meeting Victoria on her first visit to the Lviv Book Forum, and that when Kyiv was struck, Victoria was the first person to message and check she was safe. Later, when Charlotte was writing about poetry, Victoria helped her enormously. In the course of her investigations Victoria discovered that the children's author Volodia had disappeared, and dug up the war diary he had buried under a cherry tree in his garden. Charlotte suggested turning the story into a piece, and Victoria agreed. The day Charlotte finished writing it, Victoria was wounded, and she never read it. The detail shows the personal cost behind the work of cultural preservation.

[34:31] (Charlotte Higgins) **If you cannot name a Ukrainian writer, that is not Ukraine's failing** — Charlotte makes a pointed observation: the West knows Russian culture inside out — everyone knows Tolstoy and Dostoevsky — but can barely name a Ukrainian novelist, poet or painter. She admits she was the same, until she spent four years going deep into Ukraine. Her view is that this is not because Ukraine lacks good culture, but because the tides of history submerged it: under the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union, writing in Ukrainian was severely restricted, Russian was the language of education, entertainment and ambition, and Ukrainian culture was pushed into second place. The cultures of Georgia, Belarus and other parts of the former empire were pressed down under Great Russian culture in the same way. The good work is still there, but you have to go looking for it.
