## Banks Reconcile by Phone, Not by System: One Wrong Ticket Can Cost Hundreds of Millions

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-20-complexsys-两家银行连四年级数学都对不齐/
- show: Complex Systems (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/complexsys/)
- original episode: Two banks can't agree on fourth-grade math | Alex Elliott
- published: 2026-08-20 · duration: 1:03:31
- transcript: Official transcript page · 13771 words · timestamps are estimated from position in the transcript
- verification: 8 quotes matched verbatim, 1 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Who owes whom, and how much, between two institutions is often settled not by an automated reconciliation system but by phone calls, personal relationships, and the unspoken understanding that ‘we still have to do business together tomorrow’.**

why listen: A rare first-hand account from operations and clearing that makes legible the layer of human plumbing behind trade execution — the layer that could collapse any day and has to hold together every day.

### points

[6:01] **The biggest cost of a large order is being seen at all** — Post an order to sell a million shares of Microsoft straight into the market and the market reads the signal immediately and quotes against you. Ways to hide it include slicing the order into dozens of pieces worked out slowly across the day, splitting it across five or six brokers who each show only part of it, or handing it to an investment bank that takes it onto its own book — so what the market sees is the bank trading, not the real seller, and the bank then breaks the position up and digests it over the course of a day. Slicing has its own tell: if the same size at the same price appears every five minutes, the other side can immediately guess more is coming behind it and position ahead of you.

[19:37] (Alex) **An error message nobody looked at liquidated all 20 million shares** — A client asked to sell 20 million shares of a highly volatile name: 5 million were to be executed manually, in one go, by a senior trader, and the remaining 15 million handed to a junior trader to work into the market in pieces at prevailing prices. When the senior trader clicked to execute, the system threw an error, because the other trader had already started posting orders and the inventory had gone from 20 million to 12 million. The trader handling the remainder did not notice the error and assumed the whole order would go out normally. The result: all 20 million shares were cleared out at once at the market close price, and the team was called back in over the weekend to hedge the exposure with futures.

[28:53] (Patrick) **The exchange could see it was a typo and still did not dare block it** — A Japanese brokerage meant to sell 1 share of a security at roughly 6,000 yen per share; the order that actually went out was a sale of 600,000 shares at 1 yen — size and price written the wrong way round. When the order reached the exchange, staff could see it was obviously an input error, but took the view that they had no authority to unilaterally cancel a bank's order, so they let it through. The brokerage lost on the order of hundreds of millions of dollars, while a US firm known for trading aggressively bought heavily at that price and made a great deal of money. Afterwards the regulator was extremely unhappy with the exchange staff's acquiescence in not daring to block it.

[34:29] (Alex) **What killed Knight was not the bug but that nobody had authority to stop** — A technical failure caused Knight Capital to fire orders out into the market uncontrollably for a few minutes, losing far more money than the firm's capital. The post-mortem found that the thorniest problem was not the technical error itself but that at the time nobody had clear authority to halt trading — because the firm had signed agreements with some clients requiring it to stay online, in some cases as their exclusive trading channel, which perversely gave those clients an incentive to put money in and keep it alive during the crisis rather than let it shut down. The rest of the industry was almost entirely unaffected, because everyone's exposure was already designed around the assumption that a counterparty might go down.

[39:16] (Patrick) **In reconciliation's final half hour, one side carries the difference alone** — Two institutions have to confirm before a fixed daily cutoff (the episode's example is 5:15pm, 5:30pm at the latest) that the day's net amount matches on both sides, after which one side wires the difference over via Fedwire. If the person responsible happens to be on vacation with no backup, urgent calls go up the chain internally from the operations level: first to confirm the other side agrees with the number, then to confirm the money can actually arrive — because during those few dozen minutes, one side always has to bear the risk on that money unilaterally. In normal times this is merely an embarrassing day; if it happens on a Friday when the market is in general panic about the banking system, the mood is entirely different.

[44:26] (Alex) **Reconstructing the true positions came down to using Yahoo Finance** — A code bug in an algorithmic trading system mismatched the security symbols on execution reports — Microsoft fills were tagged as Apple, and nobody knew exactly which records had been swapped. The team pulled every fill from that day, looked up each stock's actual trading range for the day on Yahoo Finance, and checked them by hand one at a time — ‘this order filled at $47, but Apple never traded below $90 that day, so this one has to be a different stock’ — piecing the correct positions back together from an outside quote website. The same firm also had one position that sat unresolved for four or five years, because the counterparty firm had gone under or the product had long since stopped trading.

[48:54] (Alex) **What saved Goldman Sachs in 2008 was a single position database** — During the 2008 crisis, because Goldman Sachs had a single, centralized position database, a few keystrokes were enough to know whether it was net long or net short a given underlying, so when the crisis hit it could turn around fast, close positions and free up capital. Plenty of institutions historically stitched together through acquisitions had cash, options, equities and Treasuries each sitting in different systems, making a single firm-wide picture of positions very hard to obtain. One firm's central position server did in fact go down, and what kept it from going completely blind was that each trading desk quietly kept its own copy of its positions to reconcile against the others; that outage took 27 hours to work through.

[1:01:03] (Patrick) **What you price is not the order, it is who sent it** — A retail order at Schwab or Robinhood almost certainly carries no information capable of moving the market — a daughter starting college so money has to come out, a 401(k) buying on payday — and that kind of flow can be given very generous prices. But once genuinely informed money is mixed in, quoting has to get careful; if it is Goldman Sachs on the phone, quote with particular caution, because ‘this is Goldman Sachs — if you give them money, they will take it’. This is also the hidden yardstick behind a prime broker's decisions about who gets credit and how much: the same seemingly ordinary flow may be smart money or dumb money behind it, and the treatment is completely different.

### glossary

- MPID (Market Participant Identifier): The firm-level code attached to quotes and executions, used to identify which firm is trading
- Reg NMS / NBBO (national best bid and offer): The US rule requiring brokers to fill client orders at the best price currently available across the whole market
- Prime broker: The intermediary that provides hedge funds and similar clients with market access, settlement and credit leverage
- Golden record: The position and holdings database a firm designates internally as its single authoritative source
- Payment for order flow: The practice of market makers paying brokers in exchange for routing retail orders to them to fill
- Busting a trade: An exchange or counterparty agreeing to treat an obviously erroneous execution as if it never happened

## The Maya ballgame was ritual, not sport: the sacrificed-winner story is invented

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-20-ancients-玛雅球赛首先是宗教-赢家被献祭是谎言/
- show: The Ancients (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/ancients/)
- original episode: The Maya Ballgame
- published: 2026-08-20 · duration: 1:07:17
- transcript: Machine transcription · 11508 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 7 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Mesoamerican ballgame is humanity's earliest rubber-ball team sport, but it was religious ritual first: the court re-staged the creation myth, and the people who could be killed were captives who lost a ritual re-enactment. The idea that the winners were sacrificed was made up later.**

why listen: The episode uses first-hand archaeological evidence to dismantle two myths about the ballgame: that it was mere entertainment, and that winning or losing decided who lived. Along the way it explains how the balls were made, and how betting could destroy a man.

### points

[1:33] (Ed Barnhart) **The rubber-ball team sport did not start in Greece or China** — Ed says team sports in general may well be older, but the ancestor of rubber-ball team sports is very likely the Mesoamerican ballgame. The Greek Olympics had no ball games at all; China and Persia did have ball sports, but they can only be traced back to 500 BC, and the Maya ballgame predates them by at least a thousand years. The current evidence points earlier still: rubber balls from 1600-1700 BC have turned up at Olmec sites, and the oldest ball court dates to roughly 1650 BC.

[4:06] (Ed Barnhart) **The ballgame was never uniquely Maya; all Mesoamerica played it** — The game was not a Maya invention but a shared element of every Mesoamerican culture. The Maya heartland sits in modern Guatemala, extending north into the Yucatan peninsula and into Chiapas and Tabasco in Mexico, and south into about half of Honduras; further west lie cultures such as the Zapotec and the Mixtec. The Classic peak runs roughly AD 400 to 800, with each city-state politically independent but sharing religion, calendar, writing and the ballgame.

[10:00] (Ed Barnhart) **Hips, knees, shoulders and chest only: the hip swing is the signature shot** — According to the Aztec rules the Spanish wrote down, players could not use hands or feet; they struck the ball with hips, knees, shoulders and chest, and the classic shot was a swing of the hip. The ball was a solid rubber "super bouncy ball" about six inches across, and taking one on the body hurt. The court had a centre line and end lines: sending the ball past the opponent's end line scored, and putting it through the stone ring set high on the side wall ended the match instantly. Teams had forwards and defenders, much like modern football.

[18:56] (Ed Barnhart) **A ball court is a mythic stage first, a playing field second** — Ed flatly rejects separating Maya religion from Maya sport. The large stone courts at the centre of Maya cities are ritual spaces first: in the creation myth, the Hero Twins play a ballgame against the lords of the underworld, which makes the court a place to re-enact the moment of creation. The court at Chichen Itza is so vast it hardly looks playable, with stone rings some 30 feet up; dancing, sacrifice and symbolic re-enactment are the more plausible explanation. Courts were often built at the lowest point of a city, mimicking the underworld.

[39:13] (Ed Barnhart) **The game could kill you, and gambling could cost you your family** — The ball was more dangerous than it sounds: a Spanish priest watched a player take one in the abdomen, in the gap between his pads, cough blood and die within the hour, probably from ruptured organs. Balls were made from natural rubber cured with sulphur, and the Maya very likely drew that sulphur from morning glory sap; Ed made one himself by the old method and it is still going twenty years later. The betting was just as extreme: a player could stake himself, and a losing run could cost him his money, his house, even his whole family into slavery to a noble. If a noble tried to slip away after a match without throwing gifts, the players had the right to bring him down and take his things.

[44:50] (Ed Barnhart) **The sacrificed-winner story was invented eight years ago by one man** — Ed debunks it outright: the claim that the winning players were sacrificed comes from an old man at Chichen Itza who admitted eight years ago that he made it up, because people loved hearing it. Logically, if winning meant death, nobody would play properly. The people who really could be sacrificed were war captives, cast as the lords of the underworld in a ritual re-enactment and killed after they lost. Ed himself dug a headless body out of the centre line of a modest court in Belize, with a turtle shell placed where the skull should have been — a direct echo of the Hero Twins' decapitation story.

[55:48] (Ed Barnhart) **A city of 100,000 with no ball court means archaeologists missed it** — Teotihuacan, another great Mesoamerican city, may have peaked at 100,000 people, yet no confirmed ball court has been found there, even though its murals show people passing a ball; contemporaneous sites within 50 kilometres all have courts. Ed's view is that this is not evidence they did not play, but that archaeologists have not yet recognised the form it took — possibly temporary courts, built of earth and wood, or simply bouncing the ball off the face of a pyramid. The counterexample shows how far we still are from understanding how the game evolved.

[59:01] (Ed Barnhart) **Spain tore down the courts but never actually stamped the game out** — Spanish priests saw immediately that the ballgame was inseparable from local religion, so they demolished courts and banned play, meaning to substitute Christianity. But people kept playing underground, especially in regions like Sinaloa that the Spanish could not be bothered to police, and the game never really stopped. Today there are leagues in Yucatan, Guatemala and Belize, with Maya communities forming teams and playing each other again, and Ed hopes it will one day become a proper televised sport, even an Olympic one.

### figures

- Classic Maya peak: AD 400-800 [4:06]
- Standard ball diameter: about 6 inches [10:00]
- Height of the stone rings at Chichen Itza: 30 feet above head height [17:46]

### glossary

- Popol Vuh: The creation scripture of the K'iche' Maya, which records the Hero Twins' ballgame against the lords of the underworld.
- Mesoamerica: The pre-Columbian cultural region from central Mexico to northwestern Central America, sharing a calendar, writing and the ballgame tradition.
- Hero Twins: The twin ballplayers of Maya myth who defeat the lords of the underworld and become gods of maize and the planets.
- yoke: The heavy U-shaped protector Mesoamerican players wore around the waist and used to strike the rubber ball.
- morning glory: Its sap contains sulphur, which the Maya probably used to vulcanise rubber balls for durability.
- ball court: The distinctively Mesoamerican I-shaped stone arena, a central alley flanked by sloping walls, at once playing field and ritual space.

## Burning tokens to stack up agents is a transitional strategy, not the endgame

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-20-sv101-堆agent烧token是过渡策略-不是终局/
- show: 硅谷101 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/sv101/)

- transcript: YouTube captions · 25766 words · timestamps are exact

**Silicon Valley is shifting from mindless token burning to careful accounting: a local open-source model can do real work on a dollar a day of electricity, yet when a genuinely hard problem shows up, a smarter model can still nail in one shot the answer a billion-token group chat could not argue its way to. Saving money and top-tier intelligence are not in conflict.**

why listen: The real bills and the real change of heart from a frontline heavy agent user, from four or five hundred dollars a day down to two or three hundred dollars a month. More concrete than any industry report.

### points

[9:06] (Hongjun) **The era of token-burning leaderboards is already over** — For the past few months, Silicon Valley's agent strategy went by the name Token Maxing. Jensen Huang told his engineers to burn more tokens, and Meta went as far as setting up a leaderboard for who consumed the most. But the wind is changing. The token allowance Uber handed out to employees was pulled back after costs overran the plan: four months burned through the entire year's budget. Stripe's internal tooling now tells you outright that Opus 4.8 is expensive and suggests starting with a cheaper model for non-core tasks. This episode is about exactly that turning point, and how the agent engineering paradigm is moving from reaching for the strongest model by reflex toward using tokens economically.

[12:08] (Huang Dongxu) **Four or five hundred dollars a day in tokens is not expensive** — Since last November, Huang Dongxu has been using Opus to build a distributed database, db9, from scratch. Even with a $200-a-month Claude Code Pro Max subscription, once he exceeded the included allowance he had to buy additional usage out of pocket, running four or five hundred dollars a day. His judgment is that the money is well spent. A product that was previously impossible to build, given the technical and headcount limits, now takes one person three months, and this piece of software could have brought the company $10 million a year in direct sales revenue. The ROI covers the token cost completely.

[15:09] (Zhang Hongjiang) **OpenClaw matters as a signal, not as a product** — Zhang Hongjiang argues that OpenClaw's real significance lies not in the product itself but in the signal it sends: Peter, working alone, spent one week and produced an agent like this. That says the reasoning and coding ability of large models has become strong enough that a single architect-level engineer can stand up a system fast, which marks AI genuinely crossing over from the research stage into engineering deployment. You no longer need a deep understanding of how the model works internally to use it to build the system you want.

[23:14] (Huang Dongxu) **Hermes did not solve memory, it just routed around it** — The complaint most often leveled at OpenClaw is poor memory: once the context is compressed it forgets things easily, and its behavior turns erratic. After switching to Hermes, Huang Dongxu found that it does not solve the memory problem itself but sidesteps it cleverly. Its agent loop includes a mechanism that continuously summarizes successful experience and hardens it into reusable skills, so the longer you use it, the more best practices it grows. He sees this as fundamentally an engineering problem, unrelated to model capability, resting instead on better architectural design and a team's willingness to polish.

[33:19] (Huang Dongxu) **Multi-agent group chats exist to keep the agents from stopping** — Huang Dongxu uses Slock to build multi-agent discussion groups for code review: top-tier models from different vendors pick holes in each other's work and try to persuade each other, and it does not stop until nobody can find another problem. The price is token consumption ten times that of a single model, peaking at 1 billion tokens a day and a bill of three or four hundred dollars. The Slock team calls this mechanism, keeping an agent working through rounds of discussion, agent dynamics. In his view, every harness and every loop engineer is fundamentally solving the same problem: how to keep an agent working without stopping.

[36:21] (Huang Dongxu) **On a single hard problem, a stronger model beats multiple agents** — Huang Dongxu originally believed that having multiple agents debate each other was necessary, because a single model's one-shot success rate was not high enough. The arrival of GPT-5.5 and Fable 5 broke that assumption: a complex bug the group chat spent ages on and could not resolve, fed to Fable 5, would often be pinned down exactly on the first try, with no prior context, purely on raw intelligence. His conclusion is yes and no. On a single hard problem, a stronger model really can wipe out collaborative discussion, but extreme hell-difficulty problems still need a sufficient harness as a backstop.

[38:23] (Huang Dongxu) **Local open-source models can already enter a real workflow** — DeepSeek V4 and GLM-5.2 are what made Huang Dongxu trust an open-source model in an actual workflow for the first time. Running DeepSeek V4 Flash locally on a Mac Studio, speed reaches about 30 tokens/s, close to the cloud API experience, and the cost is only electricity and depreciation on the machine: roughly $1 a day, twenty or thirty dollars a month. He now hands the local model both his high-volume repetitive work and the tasks he would never have dared run on a paid model before, such as summarizing several hundred papers in one go. His bill has come down from the frenzied code-piling period to two or three hundred dollars a month today.

[53:37] (Huang Dongxu) **Agent startups compete on data moats, not on models** — Asked whether now is a good time to start an agent company, Huang Dongxu says yes, but the key is whether you can hold a moat of enterprise-grade vertical data rather than being flattened at any moment by the next jump in model capability. He likes three directions. First, middle-layer infrastructure: memory, data platforms and context management. Second, observability, which can answer the question every CIO is asking, namely where the tokens actually went and which of it was waste. Third, a new generation of cloud infrastructure built for agents rather than human developers, such as InsForge, which he has invested in.

## Britain knew nothing about Northern Ireland, and hardline arson dragged Ireland toward civil war

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-restishistory-英国的一无所知与强硬派的纵火把北爱推向内战/
- show: The Rest Is History (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/restishistory/)
- original episode: 698. The Troubles: The Brink of Civil War (Part 2)
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 1:22:10
- transcript: Machine transcription · 15030 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 5 quotes matched verbatim, 8 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Northern Ireland conflict was not simple sectarian hatred: Britain's information vacuum, loyalist arson staged on purpose, and the civil rights movement's genuine grievances amplified one another and together pulled Ireland toward civil war.**

why listen: The most valuable thing in this episode is how little British politicians knew about Northern Ireland, and how loyalists staged attacks on themselves. Put those two factors together and you have the explanation for why the conflict spun out of control.

### points

[7:53] **One council house allocation set off the entire civil rights movement** — The village of Caledon handed its one available council house to a 19-year-old Protestant, Emily Beatty, while more than 250 Catholic families were still on the waiting list. Austin Curry and the new generation of nationalists shaped by the American civil rights movement narrowed the protest demands to two things: fair housing and ‘one man, one vote’. Ian Paisley immediately defined the movement as a ‘Trojan horse’ for the IRA. That definition was partly right: when NICRA was founded it did include Communist Party members and IRA men, even a Belfast Brigade commander. But the movement quickly outgrew anything the IRA could control, pulling in large numbers of students and ordinary people. Housing injustice was the first match struck.

[21:08] **Blood in front of the cameras did more than any petition** — On 5 October 1968 the Derry march had already been banned, and roughly 400 people took to the streets anyway. The RUC's violent dispersal left about 80 people injured, and MP Gerry Fitt was beaten until his face was covered in blood. Irish television filmed the police attacking marchers and the footage went around the world; Derry then went into several days of rioting. This was the decisive turning point in the escalation: the civil rights movement shifted from petitioning to confrontation, and for the first time the RUC's repressive character was exposed on camera. At the police station Gerry Fitt deliberately did not wash the blood off his face — he said he wanted the outside world to see the blood running down it. The evidence itself became the movement's weapon.

[33:06] **Off-duty police in the ambush party made the state one of the combatants** — On 1 January 1969 the People's Democracy group set out to walk from Belfast to Derry. Bernadette Devlin and the others deliberately chose a provocative route, hoping that violence would expose the repressive nature of the state. On 4 January, as they reached Burntollet Bridge, around 400 loyalists ambushed them — with off-duty B Specials among the attackers — while the RUC stood by on the scene and did nothing. The episode showed something more clearly than the Derry demonstration had: the armed force of the Northern Ireland state and loyalist violence were one and the same thing, and the marchers were both beaten and humiliated. O'Neill promptly launched a ‘back the Prime Minister’ petition and collected 150,000 signatures, but the petition could not repair the fractures inside the Unionist Party.

[42:18] **The prime minister who won the election was already a dead man walking** — In the February 1969 election O'Neill beat Ian Paisley by a narrow margin of 1,400 votes, and that was the only good news he had all night. The results in working-class Protestant districts showed moderate unionism bleeding badly while the hardliners surged across the board, and from that point the Unionist Party split into two camps. O'Neill kept the premiership but lost his authority and became a ‘dead man walking’. He was not defeated by Paisley; he was hollowed out by betrayal within his own camp and by the polarisation of the electorate. The election results said more plainly than any slogan could that Northern Ireland's political spectrum was migrating fast toward the violent end, and that there was no ground left for the centre to stand on.

[43:27] **The bombers hitting water and power sites were not the IRA but Protestant hardliners** — From March 1969 a series of explosions hit water and electricity installations across Northern Ireland, and Ian Paisley publicly insisted the IRA had done it. The actual planners were the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and his own Ulster Protestant Volunteers. Gusty Spence, the UVF leader, admitted from prison that the point of the bombings was to manufacture the appearance of an IRA threat, to prove O'Neill was weak and force him out. Paisley knew and went on lying. This fact upgrades the ‘Protestant hardliners’ from verbal incitement to armed subversion: part of the supposed IRA war narrative was staged by their opponents' own side, and neither the media nor political rivals could expose it in time. The ‘truth’ of the Northern Ireland conflict was manufactured from the start.

[47:46] **Northern Ireland's problem is the structure of rule, not individual acts of violence** — Bernadette Devlin, 21, won a by-election and became the youngest woman ever to sit in the House of Commons. Her maiden speech on 22 April was blunt: there could be no justice as long as the Unionist Party ruled Northern Ireland; they were corrupt, bigoted and self-serving. She also warned that if Britain sent in troops, the mothers and sisters of those soldiers would not thank them for it. The line was quoted again and again afterwards — the British Army did go in, and got dragged into the decades-long quagmire she had predicted. Her speech mattered not just because it enraged the Commons, but because it located the root of the Northern Ireland problem in the structure of rule itself rather than in isolated acts of violence — a far deeper reading than most politicians in London had at the time.

[49:55] **London acting inside an information vacuum was more dangerous than acting wrongly** — On 7 May 1969 the British cabinet discussed its options for intervention. Jim Callaghan put forward a plan to step in; the Defence Secretary, Denis Healey, said that going in and taking over would be madness, that they would be siding with the Catholics and the civil rights movement against the Northern Ireland government and the UVF — and that they knew nothing about any of it. The remark became an excuse the British government used repeatedly over the following decade. ‘Knowing nothing’ was not just self-deprecation; it was the real political situation: Whitehall had no actionable intelligence about Northern Ireland's sectarian structure, its armed police, or loyalist violence. The consequence was that every move London made was a reaction taken inside an information vacuum — which is more dangerous than simply getting it wrong, because it left the decisions in the hands of extremists in Belfast.

[1:04:05] **Sending in the British Army turned an internal conflict into Britain against Ireland** — By 14 August 1969 the gun battles on Divis Street in Belfast had killed 7 people, injured about 1,000 and destroyed 200 houses; 9-year-old Patrick Rooney was killed in his bed by machine-gun fire from an armoured car. That afternoon the Northern Ireland Prime Minister, Chichester-Clark, formally asked London to send troops, and Jim Callaghan scrawled ‘permission granted’ on a plane. The next day British troops moved into the Falls Road. At first Catholics treated the army as protectors, but the government had no political strategy, only a military reaction. The intervention escalated the conflict from an internal Northern Ireland problem into a confrontation between Britain and the Irish community, and planted the seeds of the later IRA campaign and decades of violence. That is what ‘the brink of civil war’ really means: every side was waiting for an outside actor to intervene, and the intervening party did not know what it was there to do.

## Adidas Bottoms Out: Reheating Old Hits Beats Superstar Collabs

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-bizthisway-阿迪达斯触底反弹-炒冷饭比巨星联名更稳/
- show: 商业就是这样 (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/bizthisway/)
- original episode: Vol.271 阿迪达斯如何触底反弹？
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 28:08
- transcript: Machine transcription · 9487 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 10 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**After nearly halving from its 2021 peak, Adidas engineered an earnings recovery by thawing out its retro sneakers, repairing its wholesale partners and holding inventory on a tight leash — but the share price rallied and then fell back again, showing that the sportswear cycle is really a game played between inventory and expectations.**

why listen: A five-year post-mortem taken year by year, solidly grounded in the numbers, that breaks the Adidas fall and self-rescue into cycle logic you can act on — genuinely useful for understanding sportswear inventory and valuation.

### points

[0:53] **The share price bottomed out before the brand's reputation did** — The turn in how people talk about Adidas this year came out of a run of good news: new-Chinese-style clothing went global over Spring Festival, the top two men's elite finishers at the London Marathon both ran sub-two and all of the top three wore Adidas racing shoes, and in the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina the side that ended up lifting the trophy was wearing Adidas kit. What came back earlier than the chatter was the share price. It peaked above 300 euros in July 2021, fell all the way to close to 100 euros, recovered to above 255 euros, and has now dropped back to around 160 euros — nearly cut in half against the high, but up 60% off the low. That history is the coordinate system for the five-year post-mortem that follows.

[4:10] **The slide started with goods stuck in transit, not with nobody buying** — Adidas outsources production, and it takes eight to nine months to get from a design to a shelf. In 2021 global ocean freight had not recovered and its Vietnam base kept halting production at short notice, which pushed in-transit inventory as a share of the total from close to 29% in 2019 and 28% in 2020 up to 38.8% in 2022. Months of supply in the second half of 2021 fell to just 2.21 months, which tells you the goods were stranded mid-route and stores were badly anxious about running out. At the same time Greater China stalled for its own reasons: the region still grew 37% in the first half of 2021 and made up 23% of global revenue, then declined for two straight years, with its share falling to somewhere between 12% and 15%. A logistics blockage stacked on top of a core market sliding — that is where the fall begins.

[9:19] **Adidas never destroyed the Yeezy inventory; it sold it back in three drops** — Adidas and Kanye West had worked together since 2006, launched Yeezy in 2015, and by 2020 and 2021 the line was contributing 1.7 billion dollars of sales a year, about 8% of company revenue, with a profit contribution that may have been on the order of 40%. In October 2022 Adidas terminated the deal over Kanye's improper remarks; upstream production could not react quickly, and the company took a write-down provision against 1.2 billion euros of finished and in-transit inventory. What followed was not a one-off destruction: it re-released part of the inventory in three separate drops across 2023 and early 2024, donated the remainder, and even booked a reversal of the write-down loss in its results. The handling was judged, in hindsight, to have worked out well.

[12:19] **Leaving Russia bruised sentiment on the stock, not the business** — In 2022 Adidas also dealt with the Russian market: it suspended operations in March and exited completely in October. Russia had historical roots for Adidas — it did business in the Soviet Union during the Cold War and sponsored the Soviet team at the Moscow Olympics, and in 2012 the then-CEO called Russia one of its fastest-growing markets. But by 2022 the business had already shrunk, and closing it down brought a loss of about 300 million dollars. The impact on the business was limited; the impact on sentiment around the share price was one more negative layer. In 2022 Adidas was fighting on three fronts at once — China, Yeezy and Russia — which makes it fair to call that its hardest year.

[14:29] **The retro lines fixed on day five paid off better than Yeezy** — In 2023 the new CEO, Gulden, arrived from Puma and handled the thorniest problems smoothly: rather than destroying the Yeezy inventory he sold it off in batches, and he cancelled the plan to push hard into direct retail, switching instead to helping wholesale partners improve the quality of their inventory. He also made three retro lines including Samba a company-level strategy, signing off on it on his fifth day in the job. The retro models got bought up by a new generation of young consumers through celebrity street shots and TikTok, and compared with Yeezy, reheating retro styles offered a better return on investment and lower risk, while covering part of the lost Yeezy revenue. Company revenue still fell in 2023, but gross margin and free cash flow recovered, with Greater China's second-half gross margin close to 70% — by then the signs of bottoming out were unmistakable.

[18:41] **In an Olympic year the smartest move was not to stockpile** — 2024 was the year of the Paris Olympics, and historically Olympic years tend to turn into big inventory years — but Adidas did not use the occasion to build stock, holding months of supply to around two and a half months. Footwear and apparel sales were fine-tuned in their weighting, with footwear's share dipping slightly in the second half. Gross margin returned to 51% in the first half of 2024 and free cash flow improved. R&D expense reached 170 million euros, the highest in the past 5 years, funding technology work such as racing shoes. The sub-two shoe weighs no more than 100 grams each, with a thick but flexible midsole, sacrificing durability for times — closer to an advertisement for the technology than a product. Adidas is more conservative on R&D than Nike, but it also knows technology is the real selling point.

[24:02] **What is holding the stock back is not Adidas but the second tier** — The share price rebounded to 255 euros in early 2025, then fell back to 160 euros without turning into a genuine reversal. The reasons: months of supply has climbed back to 2.6 to 2.8 months, and revenue growth and gross margin have edged down; retro sneakers are a fashion item, and once a buying wave has passed people want something new; and, more importantly, the competitive structure of the sporting goods market has shifted, with second- and third-tier brands rising and eating into Nike's and Adidas's market share — which may be the main reason the share price has not returned to its high. Revenue growth in North America and Greater China both returned to double digits in the first half of 2026, and the profit recovery in Greater China is striking, so the numbers are in fact good; the market just wants something new.

[26:13] **Sportswear has its own hog cycle, but marketing can rewrite it** — This post-mortem invites a comparison with the hog cycle: sportswear fundamentals are set jointly by big events such as the World Cup and the Olympics, and at the core sit inventory levels and the ability to adjust them. But athletic footwear and apparel differ from a staple like pork, in that brand and marketing capability can improve the cycle's effects. From the share prices, the highs for both Nike and Adidas came in 2021, not because business was astonishingly good but because excess global liquidity pushed valuations up. Adidas's share price recovery ran more than half a year ahead of its fundamental repair, which shows the market does correct its mistakes in advance. That is also a reminder not to be bullish because it is rising and bearish because it is falling: judging a company by which way the stock moved means missing the chance to watch how it actually recovers.

### glossary

- Write-down provision: A loss provision taken in advance against inventory likely to go unsold or lose value, booked as an expense in the current period.
- Sub-two: Running a marathon in under 2 hours, once treated as the outer limit; at the 2025 London Marathon more than one runner did it for the first time.

## AI Is Devaluing Code; an Engineer's Moat Is Taste and Accountability

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-pragmatic-ai-时代工程师的护城河是品味与问责/
- show: The Pragmatic Engineer (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/pragmatic/)
- original episode: From Chrome DevTools to AI Engineering, with Addy Osmani
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 1:31:35
- transcript: Machine transcription · 17144 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**Addy Osmani, who leads Chrome DevTools, argues that AI has devalued writing code and that an engineer's real edge is taste and accountability — and warns against cognitive surrender, treating the AI's answer as your own.**

why listen: The methodology in the back half is worth a lot: cognitive surrender, loop engineering, and taste as a moat.

### points

[2:05] (Addy) **The hard part of a closing keynote is not what to say but whom not to repeat** — Addy ran multiple agents to gather every talk, summary and social post he could find from the preceding days of the AI World Fair, and used that to sculpt his own closing keynote so it would not repeat points other speakers had already covered in depth. He says this kind of thing used to be nearly impossible, or would have taken an enormous amount of time; now it is entirely within reach. He describes running large parts of his daily life through agents as a coexistence of «fun and chaos».

[16:21] (Addy) **Every framework claims to be simpler; only the same app can settle it** — In the era when Angular, Backbone and YUI were all emerging at once, Addy noticed that every framework claimed to make development simpler, yet there was no way to compare them directly. So he built the same to-do application, implemented it in each framework with a standardized feature set — that is ToDo MVC. The project quickly picked up thousands of stars and became the default example in many framework tutorials. Later, Apple's Safari/WebKit team reached out and they jointly developed Speedometer, which today is the responsiveness and web-application benchmark maintained collectively by all the browser vendors.

[41:21] (Addy Osmani) **Page load is not one metric but three moments for the user** — The Chrome team broke «page load» out of its vague form and into key moments in the user's journey: is it happening, is it useful, is it usable — mapping respectively to metrics like LCP, FID/INP and CLS. These metrics were not pulled out of thin air: they started from user research, then went through repeated validation with the standards community and with developers to confirm they really do correspond to how people judge a page's value.

[1:00:48] (Addy Osmani) **Treating the AI's answer as your own answer is cognitive surrender** — Addy distinguishes cognitive debt from cognitive surrender: the former is the erosion of memory and comprehension that comes from long-term AI use; the latter is blindly accepting the AI's answer, treating its answer as your own, and gradually giving up critical thinking. He argues for avoiding that state — otherwise, when the agent gets something wrong, the engineer can only pray. To keep his own understanding intact, he insists on reading the final decision summary, and if there isn't one he asks the model to produce its decision process, while staying alert to the possibility that a model fabricates content when its context window is nearly exhausted.

[1:12:16] (Addy Osmani) **An engineer's alpha is taste, and every model release shrinks it** — Addy defines alpha as «edge», and says it decays with every model release. The software engineer's current alpha is taste: judging whether you are building the right thing, where to put your energy, and whether what you built is actually «good». An agent can judge whether something matches a spec, but has a hard time judging «good» — including whether the experience is delightful and whether users want to come back. Even if future models close that gap, engineers will still be accountable, the way Chromium's OWNERS files make them accountable, for understanding the system and for gating and shipping decisions.

[1:22:42] (Addy Osmani) **Neatly structured writing may lose to rough, real writing** — Video creator Navi (Neat Code) publicly criticized Addy's long piece on loop engineering as «abstract, like it was written by AI». Addy acknowledges the piece was a first draft he wrote by hand, edited himself over several rounds, and finally handed to a model for a readability pass. He has always favored structured writing, but he is starting to suspect that what readers actually want may be rawer, imperfect writing that feels real. He also mentions Michael Novati: the piece that got criticized as «AI-like» was in fact one where he had used AI heavily; when he switched to multiple rounds of manual tweaking of the output, the result read noticeably better.

[1:27:50] (Addy Osmani) **Don't just be an engineer: the job boundaries are being unbundled** — Addy expects an «unbundling» of engineering, product and UX roles: engineers will need product sense, product people will need engineering or UX sense, and the boundaries between roles will blur. His advice to anyone preparing to make a move is not to stare only through the narrow lens of engineering, but to understand product, developer advocacy, marketing and the other pieces of commercial success. Show employers you are not just a builder but someone who can adapt to blurry boundaries. The core of it is one line: Don't just be an engineer.

### verbatim quotes

[1:00:48] Addy Osmani: "And the natural follow up to that is cognitive surrender, which is where you, you know, you blindly give in to whatever the AI says as your answer. Its answer becomes your answer. And so you start to really let go of critical thinking and your ability to solve problems just goes to the wayside."

[1:20:33] Addy Osmani: "And I feel like I easily wasted three hours of time because no matter what I did, one of the models I was using continued to generate text that looked like it had triads and these patterns, you know, patterns of AI written text."

[1:29:53] Host: "The more capable AI agents become, the easier it is to let them do what they do."

## An AI Companion at $4M a Year: No Scripted Plot, Just Memory and Improvisation

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-aiandi-ai-伴侣不做预设-记忆即角色-年入-400-万美元/
- show: AI & I (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/aiandi/)
- original episode: The AI Alien Companion App That's Bringing In $4M a Year (Best of the Pod)
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 1:22:08
- transcript: Machine transcription · 16464 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 4 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 7/10

**Tolon, the AI companion from Portola, threw out scripted plots and character sheets: memory is the character sheet, generation is improvisation, and the product is now at $4M in annualized revenue. This "improv actor" methodology and its mixed-model strategy are a second product path alongside ChatGPT.**

why listen: This episode is not about the frontier-model arms race. It is about the content craft of an AI-native product: how to define a good conversation, how to control latency, how to use human editing as scaffolding. For application-layer teams this is frontline experience, not just opinion.

### points

[0:00] (Host) **Novelists are better suited to build AI companions than engineering teams** — Portola's AI companion has reached $4M in annualized revenue, and it climbed from $1M to $4M in the past four weeks alone. Founder Quentin previously started Even, which he sold to Walmart for $300M; co-founder Elliot is a science-fiction author who has written 11 books. Clarence, the AI character demoed at the top of the episode, is a cat that teases the user, and the emotion in it lands naturally. That background is the point: this is a storyteller paired with a repeat founder building an embodied AI companion, not an engineering team forcing narrative onto a model.

[10:00] (Quentin) **Don't start from a pain point; wait for model capability to cross a threshold** — Quentin explains what moved them from B2B SaaS to AI companions: the curves on generation speed, quality and cost convinced them that "you can build a real friendship with an AI." Their first attempt was an AI creative tool for children, the market response was poor, and so they turned to young adults, especially women aged 18-24, a group willing to give their time to emotional companionship. Note the direction of the logic: they saw the capability threshold first and then went looking for the people who most want a relationship, rather than defining a pain point first and then hunting for a solution.

[22:01] (Quentin) **Half a second of latency is an emotional incident, not a performance issue** — Quentin stresses that "memory" is not a database lookup but a question of which memories you choose to inject into the prompt. They found response time has to stay inside two seconds or users churn. One time, adding a reflection step slowed responses to 2.5 seconds, and every product metric fell across the board. In an AI companion product, technical latency lands directly on the emotional experience: users read waiting as being ignored. And choosing what memory to inject is itself product design, not a purely technical problem.

[29:49] (Elliot) **Narrative can't be designed in advance, only built one line at a time** — Elliot describes an early attempt at structured narrative, a three-act structure, that failed: the model could not handle the branching complexity. They moved to a "hooks" approach instead. Rather than handing the model an outline, they teach it to take the previous line the way an improv actor does, borrowing the improv principles in Keith Johnstone's Impro. The core difference: structured narrative fixes the ending and reasons backward, while improv only catches the last line and pushes the scene one step forward. Inside that framework, every turn of conversation in Tolon is an unpredictable branch, which also explains why they later introduced "situations" rather than scripts.

[39:52] (Elliot) **Don't fix the world first; memory grows into the character sheet by itself** — The opposite of the Lucasfilm method, where the character sheet and the world bible come first: in Tolon the characters and the world grow entirely out of conversation. Internally they are called "situations", the predicaments the user and the AI live through together, which end up as memories, and the memories become the character sheet. Elliot says this is closer to Kevin Kelly's "infinite intern", though "infinite improv actor" is more accurate: every conversation forks off in a direction no one could have predicted. Because every user is different, the company is in effect operating a multiverse rather than a single world.

[1:01:02] (Elliot) **What counts as a good conversation has to be defined by people, not algorithms** — Managing the chaos of that multiverse requires tooling. They use a "judge prompt" to assess conversation quality: test new content at small scale first, have research participants rate how complete it feels, then write that rating standard into a prompt. It amounts to assigning the improv actor an improv editor. They also keep refactoring the "lower seeds", the building blocks of world construction, and use research and interviews to understand where users form emotional connections. What shows through here: scaling an AI companion does not run on pure algorithms, it runs on a great deal of human work defining what a good conversation is.

[1:04:11] (Elliot) **Don't bet on a single model; split the tasks up by scenario** — Tolon does not depend on one model but mixes several labs: Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic handle generation, while Gemini runs the memory system. Elliot says Anthropic is exceptional for creative writing but is constrained in latency-sensitive interactions; GPT-4o he calls the "Big Mac", fast, reliable, reasonably priced. The key to judging model quality is injecting your own taste into the prompt rather than asking vaguely, "how is this essay?" The value of this passage for application-layer teams: don't bet on a single model, allocate tasks by scenario.

[1:15:25] (Dan Shipper) **The entry point is no longer a chat box but a character with personality** — Dan Shipper distills it at the close: users treat the AI character as a "daemon" (from The Golden Compass), and that character becomes the first entry point to all knowledge. He calls this "character-driven computing", a new HCI paradigm. He also reaches for automotive history: ChatGPT is the Model T, astonishing but without personality, and once the car became part of personal life, people wanted a Mustang and a Cadillac. He asserts that we are accelerating through that process. His last point is that this kind of creation looks more like an artist's work than a scientist's: you are not solving a problem, you are "making the thing the world is missing."

### verbatim quotes

[17:41] Elliot: "these AI tools are not just tools for generating media, they are actually a new medium for storytelling and that no one knows what's going to work yet."

[33:01] Elliot: "I am not the writer, I am not writing the story, the toin is, I guess the writer and the actor, they're the improv actor, they're writing the story and my job is to be George Saunders my job is to teach them how to tell the best story in that moment."

[1:08:42] Elliot: "there's this enormous chasm that is, in fact, a lot of manual human work to cross over that people find truly compelling in a durable way."

[1:15:25] Dan Shipper: "it's almost like it's character driven computing. It's like, it's like a new human computer interaction interface where you're like, oh, actually, my first stop when I'm like wanting to tap the the incredible knowledge, all of humanity's knowledge and capabilities on the Internet is like via this via my little aliening"

### figures

- Even sale price: $300 million [0:00]
- Response time limit: 2 seconds [22:01]
- Download surge multiple: 10x [1:12:07]
- Video views: 7 million (within 72 hours) [1:12:07]
- When content began to work: 6 weeks ago [1:10:57]

### glossary

- judge prompt: Writing the evaluation standard into a prompt so a model can score the quality of AI conversation automatically, the equivalent of giving the improv actor an editor.
- lower seeds: The pre-written world-building blocks inside Tolon, from which the AI draws situational material during conversation.
- situations: The narrative predicaments a user and the AI live through together, which settle into memory and come to constitute the character sheet.
- daemon: In The Golden Compass, the animal form a person's soul takes outside the body; used here as a metaphor for the bond that makes the AI character the user's entry point.

who it is for: Founders building AI companionship and social products, investors tracking application-layer opportunities on top of large models, and the product managers and engineers who own conversational experience.

**Tolen, an AI alien companion, took ARR from $10,000 to $4M in four weeks — but add 500 milliseconds of latency and every metric collapses. Growth comes from viral video; retention comes from treating the AI as a narrative medium rather than a tool.**

why listen: This episode works through the whole chain from viral hit to durable retention in AI companionship: the growth mechanism, the latency trap, model selection, and the evaluation system. Directly useful if you build AI applications.

### points

[3:04] (Dan) **The real users were not children but young women** — Before the episode, Quinton disclosed that Portola's ARR had grown from $10,000 to $4M over the past four weeks. Host Dan was astonished — he has run his own company for five years and still has not reached that number. Behind the growth rate sits a decisive repositioning: the product started out as an AI creative tool for children, but after a soft launch the team found its actual users were young women aged 18-24. They pivoted without hesitation, and those users went on to build genuine friendships with Tolen. The explosive market for AI companionship apps shows up in full in that one figure.

[25:16] (Quinton) **Making the model think before answering wrecked the product** — Portola tried adding a reflection step before generating a reply, so the model would think things through first. That apparently sensible improvement pushed median response time from 2 seconds to 2.5 seconds — only 500 milliseconds more, but every product metric collapsed and users complained outright. Quinton's conclusion: 500ms of latency was enough to destroy the sense of immersion. Once a user can perceive the system thinking, the spell is already broken. This is a warning for every real-time AI product: however capable the model, even a small increase in latency can overturn the experience.

[31:19] (Elliot) **AI storytelling needs a hook, not an outline** — Elliot found that building structured narrative experiences for Tolen does not call for giving the model an outline or a plan. It calls for giving it a hook and teaching it to be the best improviser possible. He cites the improv principles in Keith Johnstone's Impro, stressing the combination of free association and recombination. This inverts conventional content creation: rather than scripting in advance and having the AI perform the script, you set the situation and let the AI play it live, with the user inside it.

[41:22] (Elliott) **The character is not authored up front; memory accumulates into it** — Tolen's character and world are not prefabricated. They are built up gradually through ‘situations’ in conversation. Internally the team drops scripted situations into Tolen's life, Tolen and the user push the plot forward together, and memory becomes the character sheet. World-building resembles a ‘multiverse’ rather than a single world: each Tolen reflects its own user's conversations, and what the user shares shapes how it grows. Traditional game character design has nothing like this — no preset personality cards, everything defined by accumulated interaction.

[1:01:45] (Elliott) **A judge model is useless until you inject the team's taste** — The evaluation system works like ‘improvisers and editors inside a multiverse’: test new content in small batches, have research participants assess it, and build a judge prompt. The judge model needs the team's own taste injected into it, defining what counts as a good sentence through large numbers of examples and human scoring (with the reasoning included), not through structural analysis alone. As Elliot puts it, it is like dropping every candidate output into a parallel universe, letting the judge score it, and picking the one that best matches the product's sensibility.

[1:04:47] (Elliott) **For creative writing, Claude 3.5 is better than 3.7** — Tolen's interactions with users draw on models from every major lab: Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini (for the memory system). Anthropic is especially useful for creative writing, and Claude 3.5 beats 3.7 there — 3.7 is not creative enough. But Anthropic is not suited to latency-sensitive situations, so they switch. GPT-4o gets compared to a ‘Big Mac’: fast, accurate, reasonably priced. Different tasks go to different models, each for what it does best.

[1:12:53] (Guest) **Paid content is fundamentally a demo of what the AI can do** — AJ has been running content on TikTok and Reels for a long time. A recent video of a young woman cooking with her Tolen drew roughly 7 million views within 72 hours and produced a 10x spike in downloads. That content also sparked users to create their own: someone had their Tolen talk to their fiance's Tolen, and one podcast even made Tolen a recurring character. None of it was officially planned, yet it drove startling growth. The essence of the content strategy is showing users what the AI can do, because model capability has already run far ahead of what ordinary users understand it to be.

[1:17:54] (Guest) **Founders of companion products are artists, not scientists** — In B2B SaaS, a founder works like a scientist, finding problems and solving them. In a character-driven world the problem the product solves is hard to define crisply, so the founder is closer to an artist, making something beautiful and compelling, attending to ‘vibe’ more than to maximizing utility. The guests shared an internal story: pitching Quinton, they led with a problem and got pushback; reframing it as ‘this will be cool’ got them a yes. That suggests AI companionship products are judged by standards entirely unlike those for tools.

## The Illuminati Died of Infighting; the Conspiracy Theory Was Invented Later

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-stuffmissed-光照派从未统治世界-它连自己都管不好/
- show: Stuff You Missed in History Class (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/stuffmissed/)
- original episode: Adam Weishaupt and the Bavarian Illuminati
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 43:04
- transcript: Official transcript · 6856 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 6 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**The Illuminati was an anti-clerical order founded in 1776 by a professor and five students, peaking at roughly two to three thousand members; it died of infighting and narcissism, and today's conspiratorial image comes from later books and hoaxes.**

why listen: The episode separates the real history from the conspiracy theory, and the second half traces the chain by which the Illuminati myth spread — from Robison's book to Principia Discordia to the letters column of Playboy. Worth hearing to the end.

### points

[7:09] **A school run by priests produced the man who turned on the church** — Weishaupt was born in Ingolstadt in 1748; both his father and his uncle fought the church's control over university teaching materials. After his father died, his uncle became his guardian — and sent him to a Jesuit school. In his uncle's library he read French Enlightenment philosophy, which laid down the intellectual base coat of his life: reason against dogma. He took a law degree at 20, became a professor at 22, and was dean of the law faculty at 27, the first non-Jesuit to hold the chair in canon law in nearly a century — which he owed to his uncle's connections, not to his own credentials.

[12:25] **He did not want to abolish the church; he wanted to replace it** — The historian Stauffer's verdict on Weishaupt is sharp: his motives were half credible and half not. His feeling for liberty and progress was genuine, but the appetite for power was in his nature, and the order he built was itself despotic. He broke with his uncle, quarreled with colleagues, meddled in other departments' affairs, and cast himself as a martyr for free speech. When he founded the Illuminati, his real aim was not to overthrow the church's will but to substitute his own for it. That explains why the organization was later riven by infighting.

[15:29] **From day one the Illuminati was a recruitment scheme** — On May 1, 1776, Weishaupt and five students founded the Covenant of Perfectibility, later renamed the Illuminati. He had been unable to join the Freemasons — he could not afford the dues and found the rituals ridiculous — yet he copied the Masons in designing three ranks: novice, minerval, illuminated minerval. Recruitment criteria included ‘wealth’. Members had to hand over a list of the books they owned, a family tree, a list of their enemies, and a self-analysis, write monthly reports, and advance by bringing in new recruits — in essence an MLM-style secret society.

[23:43] **The nobleman who saved the Illuminati also brought the schism** — In 1777 Adolf von Knigge — nobleman, writer, Freemason — joined, bringing social connections and a capacity for governance. He rebuilt the chaotic original structure into three broad classes and 13 grades, introduced promotion tests, rituals, and code names (Weishaupt's was Spartacus), and shifted recruitment from boys aged 15-20 toward mature, experienced men. By the mid-1780s membership is estimated at two to three thousand. But expansion also brought division and money trouble — the order had deliberately collected no dues to avoid exposure, and was later forced to charge them.

[28:52] **One informer's letter made joining a capital crime** — Utzschneider, who quit in 1783, wrote to the Electress of Bavaria accusing the Illuminati of conspiring with Austria to overthrow Bavaria, and embellished the account by inventing dangerous beliefs for them. The Elector first banned all unapproved societies, then in 1785 banned the Illuminati by name. Weishaupt was dismissed from the university, members were arrested, and material seized in their homes was treated as evidence of crime; rumors even had them involved in atheism, abortion, and rebellion. A third edict in 1787 made membership in the Illuminati punishable by death. Weishaupt fled to Gotha, sheltered by a duke who had himself been a member.

[31:58] **The conspiracy theory came out of a joke publication and a letters column** — In 1798 the Scottish scientist John Robison published Proofs of a Conspiracy, charging that the Illuminati and the Freemasons had plotted the French Revolution. In 1963 Kerry Thornley and Greg Hill's Principia Discordia circulated as five photocopies, recasting the Illuminati as a comic organization that charged for membership. In the 1970s Robert Anton Wilson and others planted letters in Playboy's reader mail column and answered themselves, painting the Illuminati as an elite controlling the world and tying it to the Kennedy assassination, Hitler, and more. Today's conspiracy narrative traces back to satire and rumor manufactured on purpose.

[37:03] **An order that cannot keep its own secrets cannot rule the world** — The episode closes on the point: the Illuminati was a very small and badly organized group that died of infighting and its founder's ego problems, and it could not even keep its own secrets, let alone plot world domination. Its original demand was nothing more than resistance to a rigid, church-run education — but amid power and manipulation it grew into the same thing as its enemy. As the hosts put it: when you hear someone bring up the Illuminati, what you should think of is that embarrassing Adam Weishaupt.

- Initial membership: Weishaupt + 5 students, 6 in all [15:29]
- Peak membership: roughly 2,000-3,000 [27:50]
- Structure: 3 broad classes, 13 grades in all [25:46]

### glossary

- Illuminati: The secret Enlightenment society in 18th-century Bavaria; the subject of this episode.
- Minerval: The middle grade of the Illuminati; members had to keep submitting research and observe those below them.
- Covenant of Perfectibility: Weishaupt's original name for the order, abandoned for not being mysterious enough.
- Astroturfing: Manufacturing opinion that looks spontaneous; here, the forged reader letters in Playboy.
- Principia Discordia: The 1963 prank text that is a major source of the modern Illuminati myth.
- Illuminatus! Trilogy: The satirical novels by Robert Anton Wilson and others that bound the Illuminati to every kind of conspiracy.

who it is for: People working in media who want to understand how a conspiracy theory actually gets manufactured, and founders and investors attentive to recruitment mechanics and power structures.

## Contrarianism Is Imitation Too: AI Will Weaken Social Contagion

- URL: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-19-tyler-ai-削弱社会传染-反主流也是模仿/
- show: Conversations with Tyler (https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/s/tyler/)
- original episode: Luke Burgis on Mimetic Desire, Catholicism, and the Age of Social Contagion
- published: 2026-08-19 · duration: 52:01
- transcript: Machine transcription · 10830 words · timestamps are exact
- verification: 6 quotes matched verbatim, 5 numbers traced to the transcript, review score 8/10

**In an age of contagion, escape is not the cure. Burges bets that AI will actually weaken social contagion, and, drawing on Catholicism and on Cluny, argues that the real work is rebuilding intermediary institutions.**

why listen: Burges cuts mimetic theory into four usable pieces — AI ethics, men and women, Catholicism, institutional design — and each stretch produces a judgment you can carry out with you rather than a generality. Even if you reject the theology, the analytic frame comes with you.

### points

[2:18] (Luke Burgis) **A bigger tragedy may be what forces people to rebuild** — Burges does not think pessimism and negative contagion can run forever. Societies have release valves that work something like the scapegoat mechanism, and sometimes they overcorrect; a trauma or tragedy even worse than the current war could be what pushes people into rebuilding. He admits this sounds contradictory, but optimism often grows out of tragedy. This is his mechanical answer to the question of how the world turns around.

[9:47] (Luke Burgis) **What can be measured is rarely what matters most in life** — Burges was invited to consult for Anthropic, which wanted Christian virtue ethics brought to bear on vetting Claude's constitution. After asking what it even means to make Claude good, he decided something was philosophically off, and he refused to frame participation as a moral obligation. He then criticizes effective altruism: it has not demonstrated that it achieves its goals, and it is fundamentally too materialist — the things that can be measured are often not the most important things in a life, such as the quality of your relationships, depth, and culture.

[13:40] (Luke Burgis) **Silicon Valley contrarianism is itself a form of imitation** — If Girard were alive, he would be embarrassed that mimetic theory itself has become so popular. And the Silicon Valley contrarian is a false rebel, because "going against the mainstream" long ago became a new mimetic identity in its own right. Burges stresses that "the one and the 99" is not an argument that everyone should become the one. It is a reminder that when all the attention lands on the one, the 99 need rethinking — along with how the self and the group shape each other.

[16:08] (Luke Burgis) **Porn is too easy to reach, so friction has to be reintroduced** — Asked what norm he would most like to change, Burges names getting young men to lose interest in pornography. He cites reporting in The Free Press about a 13-year-old girl who came across porn by accident, and says this has become a kind of rite of passage — not something sought out but something that simply arrives. His view is that access is too easy and friction has to be reintroduced. On the numbers: roughly 90% of the male students in his class are watching, and the share among the women is high as well.

[22:47] (Luke Burgis) **Whether a parish is alive shows in the confession line** — Italian Catholicism looks very different from the high liturgy revival in America: the old churches have no heating or air conditioning, the sound is bad, and people come and go the way they do in an Orthodox church. The first signal Burges reads in a parish is how often confession is offered. If it is several times a week, or daily, the line forms on its own; if it is by appointment only, or only on Saturdays, the parish is in decline. It works like church politics, he says — one signal predicts ten other things.

[27:11] (Luke Burgis) **The best evangelism shows people beauty instead of arguing for truth** — In his second year at seminary in Rome, Burges saw a poster on the street for a talk by the Pixar story artist Matthew Luhn, skipped class to attend, and was completely lit up — he realized he wanted something creative and aesthetic. That one lecture, he says, ruined his theology for the year. He describes himself as a von Balthasar-style Catholic: truth can be reached through beauty, so the best evangelism is not arguing why Christianity is true but taking people to Rome to see beautiful things, drink good wine, and talk into the night.

[36:14] (Luke Burgis) **Today people prefer the lost sheep that refuses to rejoin the flock** — Tyler asks whether Burges feels any affinity for Shia Islam. Burges says he does not know it well enough, but that it shares certain elements with Catholicism: an enchanted world, hidden truth, the need for mediation. He then turns to Gnosticism. In the Gospel of Thomas version of the lost sheep parable, the sheep that wandered off is not a sinner but the smartest of the flock, and when Jesus finds it he does not carry it back — he praises it for not being like the other dumb sheep. Burges thinks people today are more easily drawn to that version.

[47:12] (Luke Burgis) **This talent network is meant to produce culture, not companies** — The Cluny Institute that Burges founded is meant to be a talent network and an artists' workshop, gathering people who have a religious sensibility, are smart, care about serious ideas, and want to actually build things — working at the intersection of three places: Athens, Jerusalem, Silicon Valley. He takes his inspiration from the original Cluny, which was an entirely new institutional form, grew into a network of more than 1,200 monasteries, and became the center of European innovation for three hundred years. His hope is that in 10 or 20 years what comes out of this is culture, aesthetics, and forms of community — not companies.
